utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Today we'll continue with the closing arguments, and this time for the Defence. And before you start, Mr. Morrissey, I believe that yesterday you promised me to inform us about the number of that document you are going to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I will honour that promise, Your Honour, but in the preparations for closing this morning we haven't uploaded it into the system as yet, so we will certainly do that in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. And if there's nothing else that the parties would like to raise at this stage, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honour, could I just make a couple of preliminary comments. This closing address now is going to be one where I go through the broad outline of our case and explain it as best we can. Of course we rely on the brief that we filed. But, Your Honour, I make it clear that both myself and my learned co-counsel, Mr. Mettraux, are very willing and happy to be interrupted with questions if such a thing proves to be helpful to the Tribunal. And we don't need, although it's a matter for you, for you to wait until the end. If you have questions, I'm very happy to be interrupted at the time that it appears opportune to do so, and we're keen for that. I'm also told by the booth or by the -- it's been relayed to me that they don't have sufficient personnel to warn me to slow down, and therefore I'm very happy to be warned to slow down as well. Now, Your Honours, the Defence makes a submission that Sefer Halilovic is not guilty of the crimes that he's charged with here. What we submit is that the Prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt the elements of the charge that he's facing, namely murder. They failed to prove the elements of each path to liability, each path to conviction. And it's important to bear in mind that the burden rests on the Prosecutor and that the standard of proof is beyond reasonable doubt with respect to those as the Court knows very well. Your Honours, all we asked for at the start of the trial was a fair trial, and a fair trial simply means a trial according to law. This court dispenses justice, and it's very important in considering that that it is justice, generally speaking, and not justice as my learned friend Ms. Chana expressed it yesterday as justice for victims. Your Honour, justice is broader than justice for victims. It includes justice for victims, but it means a fair trial. And, Your Honour, I make the comment now because my learned friend raised that it has to be said now in response that if the Prosecution had have brought here to this Tribunal Ramiz Delalic or the killers of the victims, their comment would have made more -- would have been more apt. But as things stand, the man that they've brought to the Tribunal should not be here. He -- far from being one of the people this Tribunal was set up to deal with. He's one of the people who should be encouraged and whose conduct ought to be looked at as being a good model and part of the reconciliation, especially in a country such as Bosnia where there is a battle to get people of different ethnicity to live together and to accommodate them living together. Your Honours, in my submission to you the victims in this case would in fact be helped and supported by an acquittal. It's a terrible thing to think that at the highest level of the Bosnian army people would acquiesce in crimes like this, and it is one of the burdens that victims have to bear that not only where their nearest and dearest killed or badly treated but that it seems to have been a policy to do that. But in this case, it would comfort victims if they saw in the end and that they saw by verdict of this Court of not guilty that there was a decent person who did what he could in bizarre, unusual, and terrible circumstances. But, Your Honours, all of that is to simply say in a long way what could be said more shortly. This Court dispenses justice, and if you feel not satisfied of Halilovic's guilt, you will simply acquit him. And that's what we submit is the right verdict. Now, Your Honours, the course I'll take in this closing address is one which will go straight to the technical issues of subordination of de jure command and effective control. After that I'll address the other elements. These issues do raise -- these issues are complex in some respects, but sense can be made of them. You don't have to be frightened by the evidence. The evidence here can be explained and can be dealt with if it's faced and that's what we're hoping to do. I would like to start, however, about a remark of character and the use you can make of Halilovic's good character and the evidence of that in these proceedings. Mr. Halilovic, we say, is different; he's a different sort of accused in this Tribunal. He was positively against division, positively against ethnic hate. In our final trial brief at paragraphs 746 and following, we have set out all of the reasons why you should, having considered the evidence properly, accept that he is different and that he's unusual. How many times in this Tribunal could it be said that five days or so before the crime the accused person made a speech in public saying, We will never be a revenge army. And yet that's what Halilovic did on the 3rd of September, witnessed by the Prosecution witness Hodzic, and the reference to that is on the 23rd of March at pages 51 to 53. Hodzic described that speech as capturing Sefer's ethics of war. And that is a positive factor that you can take into account in assessing his mens rea, in assessing whether he has the relevant guilty mind. Now, in other cases, good character may be seen to have a limited or confined value. Often it's said on behalf of a general, for example, at this Tribunal that a general may have been a loyal servant of the state, may not have committed criminal offences, and may have done all they could to look after the welfare of their soldiers, often their family as well. In some respects they may look like a good citizen. But character is not of great value in those situations where such a person has participated and deliberately done so in pursuance of an evil policy, a policy of ethnic cleansing, divisiveness and death. But Halilovic is different. Because he positively did everything to stop that sort of thing. And it's very difficult to imagine another accused who is in that position, somebody who positively acted. Again, I'll make the comment. Some governments would have fine-sounding phrases within their policy. For example, the Republika Srpska certainly did have documents requiring its soldiers to respect the laws of war and so on like that. So merely because you've got a nice document in your history doesn't mean that you're a nice person or that you are of good character. But the steps taken positively of Halilovic put him out of that category of merely somebody who was going through the motions. From the bottom level dealing with normal people as he did, as reflected in Hodzic's speech, to the very top level of policy in the platform of the Bosnian government, which you have in evidence, it's Exhibit D396, and it's in the folders that have been provided behind tab number 31. Both at the bottom level and at the top level Halilovic was committed, not just in theory but in practice and in daily practice, to a good vision of a united Bosnia where different ethnic groups would live together as Bosnians. That wasn't just a political ideal, it was the ideal he held for the army and which he encouraged in the army. Those matters are directly relevant in this case. Now, turning to the specific crimes with which he's charged, Your Honours, there are certain elements that have to be proved beyond reasonable doubt by the Prosecution. I don't propose to take you to all of the elements that have to be proved concerning the crime base, and I don't propose to take you to all the elements that have to be proved concerning the crime of murder because time limits us on that. But I wish to take you to the elements hat the Prosecution has to prove and hasn't proved, we say, concerning command responsibility and concerning the other matters, the knowledge of the accused that has to be proved and the failures that have to be proved. What the Prosecution has to prove is in our submission, the following: They have to prove the de jure appointment of Mr. Halilovic vis-a-vis the alleged perpetrators; that is to say, members of the 9th Brigade and members of the Prozor Independent Battalion. The Prosecution also has to prove the effective control of Mr. Halilovic over the individuals identified as perpetrators who were members of the 9th Brigade and individuals identified as perpetrators who were members of the Independent Prozor Battalion, effective control. Further, they have to prove a temporal coincidence between effective control and the commission of the crimes. In Grabovica, the time at which the Prosecution allege against Halilovic is approximately 11 days from the 8th of September until the 19th of September. As to Uzdol, the Prosecution in their indictment appear to allege the 5th of October, but that's not sustained by evidence. What the Defence says is that Halilovic ceased to have any contact of any meaningful kind with the Independent Prozor Battalion on the 15th of September because there's no record of him having any presence in the area after that time. But other matters that place a limit on that time is a cease-fire on the 16th of September and as a matter of finality the ending of the inspection team when it reported on the 20th of September. Those seem to be the possible time periods that are open on the evidence. The next element the Prosecution has to prove is knowledge or notice that the crimes charged, in this case murders, have been committed or are about to be committed. The Prosecution also has to prove knowledge or notice on his part of the intent of the perpetrators. And at a minimum the Prosecution have to prove against Halilovic that he must have known of the substantial likelihood of crimes having been committed or being about to be committed. And I stress, and I interplay this, Your Honours, that it's not just a question of the substantial likelihood of those crimes, but there is the temporal connection. Those crimes have to be about to be committed. There is a sense of immediacy about that. And finally, of course, it has to be proved -- the knowledge has to be proved that the victims were civilians and that they were killed deliberately and the knowledge that they did not take part in hostilities. Once the relevant knowledge or notice has been established, the Prosecution have to prove voluntary and deliberate failure amounting to acquiescence of the crimes. They have to prove a failure to carry out his duties, which he had a legal duty to carry out and which he had the material ability to adopt. They have to prove the failure is gross. They have to prove also, the Defence says, that the failure was causal to the commission of the crime and that the failure entailed individual criminal responsibility under customary international law. Now, Your Honours, in that reason -- and I should stress this, too. Mr. Mettraux is going to be speaking in possibly two hours time from now, and he will give -- add more detail what I've put there, and I've put that by way of a summary at the start. Now, I wish to go now to the issue of de jure command power of Halilovic. De jure command power of course does not foreclose the whole question of effective control, but in this case we say the Prosecution pleaded a de jure case and in any event it's a matter of significance which has to be analysed. Now, at the outset the Defence says this: Halilovic did not have command power by virtual of his office. The Prosecution have conceded and they had to concede that Halilovic as Chief of Staff did not enjoy that power. Therefore, when you look at Exhibit D143, you will see the structure of the ABiH, and you will see that corps commanders answered directly to the commander of the army, as you would expect, Rasim Delic. The staffs do not command, and the law on that is clear. The facts on that are clear. Although Commander Gusic did seem to suggest that Halilovic by virtue of being number two man in the army could issue orders, that's not borne out by evidence or by doctrine nor is it the Prosecution case, and therefore you should disregard that. Your Honours, a Chief of Staff can issue orders if specifically authorised to do so. And there are clear examples of Halilovic doing just that. Exhibit number P161 is an order by Halilovic and it's an important order in the case. It's behind tab 13. Do Your Honours have those books? The Defence has prepared folders of some documents to which we shall refer. Those documents will also come up on the screen in e-court, but some of these documents are going to be referred to from time to time and it may assist if we look at that one -- just a moment. We have a problem. Behind tab 13 is the order by Halilovic, Exhibit 161. Now, that order is an order to Karavelic. And when you look at it, you'll see it's signed "Chief of Staff." The comment it has the words "deputy commander" written in there, but we know because of the doctrinal use of the term "zastupa" that that was not signed in his capacity as deputy commander and it's not suggested otherwise by the Prosecution. So looking at that order there, you can see it's an order which appears to be a command. It says "order" and it directs Karavelic to do certain things by way of releasing troops. Now, it's an important order, but the focus at the moment is on what -- how Mr. Karavelic responded to it. Karavelic receiving that order did not obey it straight away. He went and checked that order with Commander Delic. And he did that because Halilovic was Chief of Staff. Halilovic could only issue such an order if specifically authorised by an order from Commander Delic. Karavelic questioned that order, and Commander Delic authenticated and said and told him, Obey the Chief of Staff's order. Now, Your Honours, therefore orders issued by Halilovic have to be analysed carefully because you have to be sure that he's issuing the order under his own power before you can use it to make a determination or draw an inference that he's got some command power, and in that case the specific evidence is he did not. Because he had had -- because the person who he directed it to went and checked and felt able to go and check with Delic, nor did Delic say to Vahid Karavelic, You don't have to ask me, just obey the order. Instead he gave him the direction. Your Honours, Halilovic was specifically limited in his powers. I won't take you to Exhibit D143, but the evidence about it was clear that he had unusually limited powers as Chief of Staff. And I'll get a little bit later on to what we say was an official campaign to undermine Halilovic's power at the time. Your Honours have in evidence - I haven't put this in the book - Exhibit D244, which is that transcript between President Izetbegovic and the president at the time of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, where after Halilovic was demoted President Izetbegovic said to Tudjman, Look -- he -- we've set out the whole quote in our brief, of course, but he said, He will not be able to do anything. Now, Your Honours, there's a couple of other short points to make about the Chief of Staff and the powers that Halilovic had by his office. He was, by virtue of D143, a deputy commander of the Bosnian army. But the Prosecutors have explicitly agreed that he didn't exercise any de jure power as a result of that appointment and that's obviously correct, so I don't need to take that any further. The Prosecution did at one stage raise the issue of Halilovic being the most senior person in the area. We've dealt with that in the pre-trial -- in the brief as well, but I ask you to consider Exhibit P106 and point 16 of that which indicates that this doctrine of the most senior commander present is an emergency, unusual doctrine, and it hasn't been proved to be a power under which Halilovic operated during these -- on these occasions. Your Honour, that ends, if you like, the formal -- the powers that Halilovic had by his position. So what that means is: The Prosecution had to prove an appointment of Halilovic, they had to prove an appointment by order. He doesn't have any power by establishment or by rank, the Prosecution have to prove that he had an appointment by order. Your Honours, there is a section later on concerning the undermining of Halilovic, but it's worth mentioning now some features. It's very unlikely that either President Izetbegovic or Commander Delic would appoint Halilovic to command authority. First of all, you have hat transcript where Izetbegovic makes it clear that that's exactly what he isn't going to do. Exhibit D437 is that document whereby the Minister of the Interior, Bakir Alispahic, placed Halilovic under surveillance. Could I just indicate to Your Honours, I'm going to refer to many exhibits which are not in that folder. The Exhibits that are in the folder are simply ones which are -- which are worth looking at at this stage and which we have time to look at at this stage. Exhibit D437 is discussed in the brief, of course But Halilovic was placed under surveillance as -- as effectively an enemy of the state at that time. The idea that he would in those circumstances be appointed to a command function with troops who the gossip and the operative information were saying were loyal to him in some form is an untenable assertion. You would really need very strong evidence. And in that regard, the tendered witness statement of the deceased Iset Mustafic is quite an important document. The claims that Mustafic makes would have been surprising ones in isolation. If he just said, look, there was an undermining campaign without anything to corroborate, you would be entitled to regard that with caution and look to see if there was corroboration. But on the evidence in this case it's just overwhelmingly clear that there was such a campaign. Because when you look at how Halilovic was treated by the officers, one in particular we'll come to later is a man called is Fikret Pravljak. It's quite clear that Halilovic was being undermined. However, more of that later. At the moment we turn to the indictment, and paragraph 3 of the indictment the Prosecution explicitly pleaded an appointment by Halilovic to command of the Operation Neretva 93. They relied on three things to do so. They said at the Zenica conference Halilovic was appointed; they also relied on the order of the 30th of August, which is the famous order in this case, and it's Exhibit D146; and there's a third document which the Prosecution say constitutes evidence of Halilovic being appointed, that's the map, D131, Exhibit D131. Now, Your Honour, the Defence says that that evidence proved to be a disaster for the Prosecutors, and it really proves the opposite of what the Prosecution contend. All the Defence has to do in terms of this Tribunal is to raise a reasonable doubt on that topic because it's an element of the offence or an important fact in the offence that he was appointed. The Prosecution would have to prove that beyond reasonable doubt. So that the Defence only has to raise such a doubt, but in fact what we submit is that it's not a question of doubt that the evidence is absolutely overwhelming that there was no appointment. When you turn to the Zenica conference, this is something that been quietly dropped by the Prosecution. They no longer say what was said in the indictment because the indictment makes it clear that at the Zenica conference certain things happen. But unfortunately the evidence proved otherwise. A witness who was hostile to Halilovic was Commander Gusic and he said that no such thing happened at Zenica. Karavelic was there, he said no such thing happened. The cameraman, Mr. Glavas was there, and he says no such thing happened. He took a video of it and the video shows that no such thing happened. And there is a transcript in evidence, which is D405, and that is behind tab 32. I'm not going to ask you to go to it now. It may arise later, but it's there just in case. There was no appointment on that occasion. And the evidence therefore of Witness Alispahic about that ought to be regarded with the gravest caution because he appeared to base his conclusions about Halilovic being a commander on that Zenica conference and also on a resubordination of some of his troops, the Lasta unit, which you will recall, which we proved did not happen by exhibits. Your Honours, the Zenica conference does not provide an occasion when Halilovic was appointed appointment and it's dead. In fact, it seems to suggest the other thing because Halilovic did not talk at that conference at all about this operation. What he talked about was capturing a munitions factory at Vitez. We turn to the order of the 30th of 8th and that is behind tab 6, and I'll just ask that we go to that very briefly. Your Honours have a very full analysis of that in our brief. The Defence went to the detail; the Prosecution didn't. Why is that? Because the detail supports the Defence quite clearly. Your Honours, commanders are appointed. There is no dilemma about appointing commanders. We have examples of command appointments at Exhibit P -- I'm not going to take you to these but I just assert them. P102. Defence Exhibit 144 and also Defence Exhibit 193 are examples of appointments where it is absolutely crystal clear when you appointment a commander to a command. Commander Delic could have done that; he had that power. He chose to make Halilovic the leader of an inspection team. That choice is itself a significant thing to do. It is true that inspection teams can be given quite a wide range of powers, but you don't need that subtlety if you are appointing someone as a commander. The appointment to an inspection team indicates quite strongly what the contemplated role for Halilovic was. When you come to the terms of that order you can see it supports the Defence contentions in terms. You don't need to be too subtle about this. I want to make the comment in advance. The Prosecution did not call expert evidence about this. The Prosecution said in -- in argument yesterday that the Defence was missing the big picture here, but really you've got to come to grips with the evidence. If the Prosecution want to call a de jure case, they should prove it. It's not a question of big pictures when you're dealing with de jure appointment. It's a question of law, legality, the orders. And when you look at this order, that's why the Prosecution pleaded the big picture, Your Honours, because they can't do anything else. If they go to the details it falls upon them. If you look at the preamble, the preamble sets what the terms of reference of this inspection team were. The Witness Cikotic on page 61 on the 23rd of February said that the preamble was a legitimate basis to interpret this order. Of course, and that stands to reason. Now, as trained lawyers and professional Judges, whilst you benefit from expert opinions on things, interpreting documents like this is not tremendously difficult to do, and when you look at it, it keeps telling the same story. At point number 2, or prong number 2, Halilovic's role is captured. He's not commanding anything. He's the leader of an inspection team. At point number 3 you can see that he is given a limited power to issue orders. Now, that's a very real power to issue orders, and there were occasions when he did issue orders under that power. I'll give you an example. P124, which we'll come to later on, was an order on the 15th of September where he gave an order concerning reorganisation on the spot of the 317th Brigade and elements of the Prozor Independent Battalion. Another example of that power, we submit, is when he told Buza to go into battle in compliance with the order that Buza already had from his own corps commander, something else we'll come to. But it was an emergency power. And it's very important to note that limited power because if he was the commander there was no need to give him that power. If he had command power, he didn't need point 3 in that order. You can't reconcile a general command power with point 3. Point 4 signifies the end of the inspection and makes it quite clear that that's an inspection team. That's important from another point of view because it puts at end to any command power Halilovic is said to have had under this order and that is really all the Prosecution have got to go on, so that we say that this -- any liability of Halilovic of any sort in this case ends on the 20th, even if you found everything else the Prosecution asked you to. So now coming back to point 1, you can now interpret what that power of "rukovodjenje" that was given to Halilovic means. Because it doesn't exist on its own; it exists in the context of the order and it's to be so interpreted. The word itself has got many shades of meaning. It's a general term. But what was important was the evidence of Selmo Cikotic who said that a staff -- sorry, pardon me, that staffs can participate in "rukovodjenje." Now, Halilovic in this order is specifically identified as a Chief of Staff, so that when the Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic, is given a power of "rukovodjenje," that does not mean he's given a power of command. Because staffs do enjoy a power of "rukovodjenje." Your Honours, at paragraph 244 of our final brief we made it quite clear of what our interpretation of that order is. The Witness Karic made it clear that his interpretation of that order was that Halilovic was not given command power by Delic. Jusuf Jasarevic said on the 1st of March, at page 69, I don't see that Mr. Halilovic is commander of the operation. Prosecution argument on that topic, in my submission, is poor because they rely on the report of the inspection team later on, but no where in that report do you find that inspection team saying that they commanded, nor do you find the term "komandovanje" in it. Your Honours, it really was a necessary shift in the Prosecution case that my learned friend Ms. Chana argued. They had to argue that the de jure and the de facto case blurred together and need to argue that now because the de jure case, we say, is not merely beset by doubt but is absolutely proved to the contrary. Turning to other documents relevant to this question, the map, which is D131, is behind tab 4. Your Honours may have a look. It's only the small -- reduced version, I'm sorry to say, but there you'll see it. And on that map prima facie is some very important evidence from the Defence point of view. In the top left-hand corner, one can see Rasim Delic signing that map as commander, and in the bottom right Sefer Halilovic signs it as Chief of Staff. Now, those terms are quite plain, sensible terms; they mean what they say. And witnesses treated them as doing so. It's quite true that that map itself doesn't rule out that Halilovic could in theory be given other command powers later on; of course he could. Karavelic made it quite clear that he wasn't comfortable to say that just because of that map that that proves that Delic was commander and Halilovic wasn't. Because it was always open to Delic to give Halilovic power. The focus, however, has always got to be on this: There has to be an order. Delic has to have ordered Halilovic to become a commander. And if he didn't give such an order, Halilovic isn't the commander. And, Your Honours, because of that you have to ask the question: Why isn't there any such order in evidence? And you have to ask the next question that follows from it: Why isn't there a reference to any such order in other orders? Sometimes an order might get lost. In archives an order may not -- may be misplaced or somebody else might misplace it. You just never know what might happen to a single document. But in the case of an order making Halilovic commander, and I interpose this, if such an order existed, the authorities in Bosnia, you might expect, would have found it very quickly. Very quickly. But there's no reference to such an order in other orders. Look at the combat plan of Zulfikar Alispago later on, when he issued an order to go into battle; it's exhibit D273. He said, I order the commencement of Vrdi 93, defence of people's rights. There's not a reference at all to Halilovic, to Neretva 93 or to any order appointing Halilovic to any power. And what we submit is that when you look at the doctrine concerning maps, which we just don't have the time to go into here, but if you look at the Exhibit P106, look at points 493, 498, and 501, and you will see that there is sound doctrinal support for the proposition that a map can constitute an order. And in this case of course it was an order that was obligatory on Halilovic. Halilovic on anyone's view is subordinate at all times to Delic. I suppose I'll put it in very formal Defence terms. The Prosecution didn't prove beyond reasonable doubt that Halilovic was appointed to command. But what we're saying is that you could go further than that. You could make a finding that Delic deliberately reserved power to himself. It shouldn't happen in pure military terms, but that's just not the way Bosnia was and that's not the way the army was. There's a couple of other things that I'll deal with very quickly in passing in relation to that. The Prosecution at one time alleged, and it was alleged in the opening which we made clear at the time and we make it clear now, it was a very compact and concise sensible opening, putting the Prosecution case the best way it could be put by Ms. Chana. But in that opening the operations group was mentioned. Now, it's not pleaded elsewhere. It's a new arrival on the scene. The reason why it arose, you might speculate, is that the Prosecution needed a structure because they don't have Mr. Halilovic being appointed to command any troops or to deal with any organisation over any specific time or in any specific area. And hence, the Prosecution at one time flirted with this idea of the operations group. However, the evidence was crushing on that point also that there was no operations group. There needs to be an order to set it up; there wasn't one. In our brief at paragraphs 251 to 255, that is dealt with. I'll say no more about it. The Prosecution relied upon the existence of an IKM in Jablanica to help found an inference that Halilovic must have been appointed as a commander. It doesn't have that effect, however, because there's a reasonable open competing inference arising from what Mr. Karic said, a Prosecution witness, who you might regard as a reasonable and sensible witness who testified here despite ill health. Mr. Karic was not a blame-shifter and was not a person who tried to minimise his role. Mr. Karic in fact said, I am the man who billeted those troops in Grabovica. He's not to be viewed, unlike Commander Gusic, as someone who's trying to hide his own part in the proceedings. Quite the reverse. He admitted it. So you can give his evidence some significant weight. And Karic made it quite clear at that time this IKM was called an IKM because we didn't know what else to call it. They could have been led into that era by the fact that they did have and obviously did have some limited command power. They were a hybrid, unusual, weird team. The powers in the inspection team have been testified to be slightly broader than the usual inspection team powers, and that's clear on the face of it because it has that limited command power in point 3. However, if the Prosecution wish to use the existence of an IKM as a basis for an inference, then they should be compelled to demonstrate to you by proper evidence - and in this case it should have been expert evidence - what an IKM was in the Bosnian army in 1993. It is no use to presume that IKMs mean the same thing across systems. The evidence about the Bosnian army is that it was an immature army, the structures of which were not sound and in short you needed to know what it meant. You needed direct evidence as to what it meant. And the IKM is a blind alley in this case. It could be the subject of hours of discussion. We're not suggesting the Prosecution deliberately left it vague blame for obfuscation. But what we're suggesting is that they didn't prove what an IKM stands for and what it means. And on a doctrinal basis, there is one important point to remember. An IKM is a derivative command post, and if you don't have a central command post you can't have an IKM. And the Defence says that the central command post in this case must have been in Sarajevo. Your Honours, there's nothing less riveting than the subject of IKMs and it's now finished. I want to put the proposition now you could accept that Commander Delic specifically and deliberately retained command power and specifically and deliberately did not release such power to Halilovic. It might be seen as a passive move by Delic, a denial of Sefer Halilovic's powers, and it's not necessary for you to find that Delic therefore took a more active role than the evidence shows in Neretva 93. The effect, however, of what Delic did was to undermine Halilovic's ability to effectively control the troops. The signs of Delic doing this are quite clear. First of all, there is no order about Operation Neretva 93. And that's a puzzling thing if Halilovic was the commander, but it's not puzzling if Delic retained ultimate command power over it because there doesn't need to be an order appointing Delic. Secondly, the map. There was evidence that a map should be accompanied by a big, thick dossier consisting of orders and various attachments. But no such order exists, nor was -- nor was it referred to in any other documents. And the reason for that, too, is that there's no need for it if Delic retained command power. There is no dilemma that Delic had such power. Look at Exhibit D143. He was the commander of the army with direct command to command all of the units that were involved in this incident. Commander Delic was involved in combat there. We've listed in the final brief at paragraphs 271 and following that Delic had an involvement in previous command -- previous combat in that area. Exhibit D406, I'm going to come to again that later. It is behind a tab, and I'm sorry, I just haven't noted the tab here. But Exhibit D406 indicates clearly that Halilovic was -- sorry, that Delic was in discussions -- just excuse me, Your Honours, I'll find it. It's D33. It's behind tab D33. It might be appropriate to go to that now very quickly. Now, here -- this was the inspection team, Zicro, Rifat, and Vehbija - and you can conclude that means Suljevic, Bilajac, and Karic - have written not to Halilovic but to Delic. And in the final words, the second-last sentence, they say: "We do not know if the proposal that we have sent to use units from Sarajevo and the 3rd Corps met with approval." That's a letter to Delic. Delic obviously was involved in the selection of these troops and had to be. The 92 bis statement of Mr. Pejanovic made it clear that Commander Delic left for Herzegovina at that time. I've already pointed out that the order, Exhibit P161, that's Sefer Halilovic's order on the 2nd of the 9th behind tab 13, was an order specifically backed up by Commander Delic. Delic attended at Donja Jablanica, the base of Zulfikar Alispago, which is where most of the main meetings seem to have taken place despite the alleged importance of the IKM. And at Zuka's base on that day he signed the map and wrote the word "odobravam" above it. Delic also received reports from Zuka. Why was he receiving reports from Zuka if Zuka was directly subordinated to Halilovic? We have direct evidence of two of those. One of them is the report that Zulfikar Alispago said he was going to send to Delic, and we have no reason to doubt that he did so, but that's not strong evidence that he really did send it, so he just expressed it intentionally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We kindly request that the counsel slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm now going to slow down. As to Zulfikar Alispago, therefore, you have evidence that he regarded himself as being liable to report to Delic. And that was backed up further by the infamous helicopter order, the subject of which was irrelevant. It was about combat, it was a combat report, and it had a focus on a helicopter. That document is Exhibit D201. You don't need to look at it but you can if you need to. How can it be that Halilovic is being bypassed if he's the commander? It cannot be. The 6th Corps reported to Delic. Look at the investigation into Uzdol. They reported directly to Delic. Look at the investigation into Uzdol. They reported directly to Delic. The 4th Corps reported to Delic. Look at the statements of Mr. Budakovic, Mr. Najetovic. There is no difficulty about this. Those units reported. And particularly important is the 4th Corps. This operation was about Mostar. That's where the 4th Corps were. How can it be that Halilovic, commanding those units, did not have anything to do with the 4th Corps in that time? But the answer's resolved if Delic retained command power for himself. In that way, coordination between the two parts of the operation is maintained. Finally, we make the comment that the Prosecution withdrew Commander Delic and his deputy Stjepan Siber as witnesses. Now, they are entitled, as the Prosecutor, said in the exercise of their discretion to withdraw whoever they wish. But they can't both have their cake and eat it. They can't not call those witnesses but still ask you to draw an inference in favour of those people. And Mr. Delic could have said what the Prosecution inference -- the inference the Prosecution ask you to draw is that Halilovic was the commander. But they weren't prepared to call Delic. Now, I'm not criticising them, it's not a question of cheating at all. It's not like that, but it weakens their ability to rely on an inference contrary to that. Why not get him here, let him say it isn't so. They don't. The next thing the Prosecution rely on is orders as evidence -- orders as evidence of command. This is taking too long, Your Honours, and I'm going to speed it up. The Defence says that the orders issued by Halilovic are explainable under the powers he had. We've identified the sources of those powers: The order of the 30th and his power as Chief of Staff. It was a power that he had under the order to issue emergency orders. The instructions, the drafts that he prepared in -- at other times were as Chief of Staff. They were always signed as Chief of Staff. Not once had the Prosecution produced an order which is signed by Halilovic as commander; there isn't one. They're all signed as Chief of Staff. Of course the Prosecution in its submission - it wasn't deliberately misleading of course in their final brief but it had the effect of looking misleading unfortunately - suggested that Halilovic issued those orders as commander of Neretva 93. And what I ask you to do is to look at the orders and you'll see that he doesn't do any such thing at any time. Now, time forbids me to go through these matters. I'm just going to move on from them. But that's the conclusion that we submit. We submit to -- and finally, it's an important point -- what we submit is that the Prosecution have sought to get you to draw an inference from orders by other people. So that they've pointed to orders by Karavelic, and the Prosecution have invited you to look at those orders by Karavelic and say, well, look, Karavelic thinks that these units are going to be resubordinated to Halilovic or at least that they will receive tasks or orders from Halilovic. There's two things to be said about that: The first is the realistic one. Karavelic himself made it clear that the power Halilovic had to command those orders depended on what power Delic gave him at all times. Karavelic did not know what the content of that power was, of course. But secondly, as a matter of form, as a matter of de jure power, those orders by Karavelic, the orders to a lot of people, cannot in themselves as a matter of law determine Halilovic's status. They don't have that power. Delic has that power. Karavelic doesn't. No one can change Halilovic's status or give him command power but Delic. And if Halilovic issues an order, as he did on the 2nd of September, all that means is that he was authorised to do so by Commander Delic. And it doesn't allow you to draw a conclusion that he was appointed as a commander, nor does it allow you to draw any conclusion as to his effective control. And perhaps I just underline this. The claim that I was referring to is in the Prosecution final brief at paragraph 182. I want to turn to the actual relationships now which the Prosecution have got to prove. First of all, the Prosecution have sought to prove that Halilovic exercised effective control because he had de jure power through a chain of command extending down to -- through the Zulfikar unit to Ramiz Delalic's troops. I'll deal now with that line of subordination. There's an absence of a formal appointment; that's important. The Prosecution de jure case is, we apprehend, and Mr. Re said it yesterday, is that the Zulfikar unit was subordinated to Halilovic, and the 9th detachment was subordinated to Zulfikar. Well, there's no order to that effect. The comment I referred to by Karavelic saying that Halilovic's power depended on what Delic gave him is at page 41 on the 20th of April. Zulfikar Alispago was an independent agent. He was not obedient. He remained a separate detachment of the Main Staff. His order, D273, that's the combat order of the 11th, represents his independence. Karic made it clear that Zulfikar Alispago disposed of the proposed order given to him by the team and simply shredded it and drafted up his own one. Your Honours, the subordination to the 4th Corps failed because time is going -- I'm going slower than I thought, I'm not going to take you to tab 34. If you can look at the comparison between Exhibit 120, which is where Delic tried to resubordinate Zuka, and Exhibit 443 where later on Delic said, I failed. I just didn't happen. You try to resubordinate Zuka's unit to a corps but it just doesn't happen. Your Honours, it was suggested that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and the 9th Brigade were resubordinated as well, but frankly that just is not proved to have happened. There's no evidence at all that the 9th Brigade regarded themselves as -- or were as a matter of law resubordinated to the Zulfikar unit. There was an order in evidence, it's P121, where the Sarajevo units are said to be resubordinated to Zuka's unit. That wasn't an order. That's a draft that is sent from Jablanica up to Mr. Halilovic. It was put forward by the Prosecution as being an order by Halilovic, but you know from looking at that order, as you did during the trial, that that order was sent from Jablanica by the staff to Halilovic. The face of the order makes it clear. It's not an order by Halilovic at all. It's not signed by him, and it was sent to him in Sarajevo by the staff back at the IKM. All right. As to the formal line of resubordination with the Independent Prozor Battalion, there is no difficulty about that whatsoever. That Independent Prozor Battalion was argued by the Prosecutor to be resubordinated to Halilovic. They say it was taken out of the 6th Corps and placed -- and resubordinated to Halilovic. That's the claim made by -- with the Witness Salko Gusic. However, the answer here is very easy. Behind tab number 7 you will find Exhibit D149. And Exhibit D149 tells you which order Buza was obeying when he went into battle at Uzdol. It tells you it clearly. There are no difficulties about this at all. He nominates an order which has got an order number 01/1500-27. That order is in evidence, too; it's behind tab number 10. And behind tab 10 you will see an order from the 6th Corps, not an order from Halilovic. Buza himself regarded himself as being bound by a 6th Corps order and acted in accordance with it, and fortunately we've got that order in evidence. Therefore, the argument that Halilovic had the Independent Prozor Battalion resubordinated to him is dead because we know who Buza was resubordinated to -- who Buza was subordinated to and it was his own normal commander. But the Prosecution relied on Salko Gusic to say that that had happened. Now, Your Honours, Gusic was a bad witness, and it's the Defence policy that we won't make a comment about a witness unless we can bear it out and demonstrate where it is that you should find fault with a particular witness. Now, he was a witness who had a motive to tell the -- to shift responsibility, namely, that he doesn't want to be placed in the line of command and control himself. Therefore, he told the story that Halilovic had been resubordinated. However, when you look at the evidence, you'll see he was right in the middle of it. First of all, the order binding Buza, D152, is a 6th Corps order. Secondly, you have behind tab 9 Exhibit D151 which is a letter from Kovacevic of the 44th Brigade. This is a brigade where -- this is a brigade that was involved in the combat, and Sevko Hodzic gives details about how one of its members was killed. There, Kovacevic is writing to Gusic directly and clearly indicating, I'm expecting you to come and help me like you said you would. Witness J at page 12 on the 6th of July made it quite clear that the Prozor Independent Battalion stayed in the line of command and control of the 6th Corps. The Prosecution's argument on that topic is, in my submission, finished. Of course they might rely on the two orders issued by Halilovic, namely an oral order -- an order instruction to go into battle in accordance with the order that he already had and also at P124. But as we've said, both of those are an exercise of the emergency power that Halilovic had. Your Honours, I've taken too long on the topic of the de jure issue, but I wanted to demonstrate two things this doing that: First of all, the Prosecution didn't prove their case, and secondly the Defence, we submit, positively proves the contrary. You can act on the basis that Halilovic was not formally appointed as commander of anything. It's not just a question of expressing a doubt. You could make the finding here that Delic denied Halilovic effective power, that such power as he gave him did not allow him to exercise effective control. Now, Your Honours, because it's quite intense and because of time management issues, I would ask that -- although it's only been one hour, I would ask perhaps if we might take a short break now. Although it is earlier, it will help with time management. Because I have spent more time on it than I want to, I would just like, if I may, to break briefly and restructure certain issues -- certain of what is to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you believe that is feasible and practical for us to have a break now, we are entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But the total amount of time will remain unchanged. Yes, we'll take a break and we'll resume at 10.30

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that our interpreter and the court reporter has done a wonderful job, but however I have to remind the Defence to slow down so that to take the consideration the difficulties they are facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd just indicate I'm very grateful for the help we get in that regard and I'm, as always, very happy to be told to slow down including by my own team. Are Your Honours ready for me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just indicate that that last section, although it took 56 minutes and was quite lengthy as a result, is important because it provide, first of all, unless the Prosecution proved that Halilovic was appointed de jure, we say that's the end of the case. And that's in the heart of the Prosecution's own case. That's right in their own fortress, if you like. It's something that they should have been able to prove easily, but because of the difficulties they didn't prove it. Of course effective control is where the focus has to be. But the absence of a clear order appointing Halilovic to de jure control is a very important factor in assessing effective control, and that's how you should treat it. Of course we maintain our pleading position that if they don't prove de jure control, that's the end. But in the alternative we make it clear that it's relevant in that way. I wish now to go to effective control. I can indicate that this segment now will be less -- will less technically intense and perhaps have a more direct connection to the chronology of the case and to the evidence that bears on what actually occurred in it. I want to make a couple of general points about effective control as it relates to Halilovic. The first point is that it was hard for Halilovic to exercise effective control over anyone. I'll come to why. And secondly, that effective control generally in Bosnia at that time was hard to exercise, not impossible, it's not to be ruled out that people could be in effective control of units, of course they could be. But it's a relevant matter for you to assess. Now, let's just go to the details of each point. As to Halilovic's exercising effective control, it has to be borne steadily in mind that he was a suspect person, according to the government. There is no doubt he was under surveillance. He was demoted by Exhibit P102. He was surveilled because of Exhibit 437. He was undermined according to the Witness Mustafic. And Mustafic told a story concerning the commander of the 4th Brigade at Hrasnica. That's the brigade that sat outside the tunnel. And you'll remember that when Sefer Halilovic went with the journalist Hodzic to go down to the battle zone on the evening of the 7th of September and into the morning of the 8th, he went out there and he couldn't manage to arrange transport for his troops because Fikret Pravljak wouldn't give him the trucks. And that's detailed at length in Hodzic's book, and it was given in evidence here as well. Now, Karavelic, Witness Karavelic gave you some evidence about Pravljak. He was a man you just couldn't get rid of, because despite wanting to fire him he seemed to enjoy patronage at the highest level. He couldn't be moved. Halilovic was clearly obstructed by Pravljak. And then when you find that Mr. Mustafic's statement, says that Pravljak was one of the people that he dealt with in terms of the undermining campaign, this is the evidence from different sources coming together to show an unescapable [sic] conclusion, and that is that Halilovic really was being undermined. That doesn't determine the question but it's important background when you're assessing whether he was capable of exercising effective control. You already know that he was a weak Chief of Staff, a particularly weakened one. You already know that Izetbegovic transcript. You know that Halilovic constantly complained during the time he was in Herzegovina of obstruction, in particular with respect to Commander Gusic of the 6th Corps who, Halilovic felt and thought, was avoiding him and making life difficult for him deliberately. That was borne out by the Witness Karic, who in his deposition which is Exhibit D44 -- sorry, P444. At page 104 of that document, Karic himself supported that viewpoint that Gusic was undermining and obstructing and not meeting when he was supposed to meet. In the end Commander Delic had to issue an order to Gusic, grow up and meet the Chief of Staff, please. And, Your Honours, again, it's an ineffable thing. It's not a doctrinal thing. It doesn't prove or disprove that he had effective control, but it definitely weighs in the balance. The situation in the Bosnian army generally is relevant. My learned friend Ms. Chana, in a picturesque phrase, it was a very accurate one though, when she said it was held together by spit. The truth is it wasn't held together by the normal line of command and control because it couldn't be enforced. In order for a normal -- I'll just take a step back from that. In a normal army people obey orders. If they don't obey orders they are dealt with. There is a sanction, there is a punishment. It could be demotion, it could be put in prison. There are more extreme situations that could develop. In Bosnia that just didn't happen in those days. There just wasn't the ability to do that. The command and control system was immature. You've seen the evidence about how that army effectively came to be an army and it was at Trebevic. It was when the army finally dealt with Ramiz Delalic. That's when it became an army because at that point it called to account insubordinate people. Before that, Delalic got away with it without sanction. The 10th Brigade effectively, we're going to submit later on, are effectively irrelevant to these proceedings but it's illustrative that Musan Topalovic, Caco, the commander of that brigade got away with it for months, simply refusing to do anything, threatening to cook the commander of the 1st Corps on a spit and generally indicating that he had no intention of complying with orders and he just did it and got away with it. Now, you can draw a conclusion from that that there was no effectively sanction. That has an impact on the ability of Halilovic to exercise effective control. A lawfully sensibly appointed commander, Vahid Karavelic of the 1st Corps, with respect to whom there was no doubt about his ability to issue commands, could not issue commands. As he said, you had to ask people nicely. Halilovic didn't have the security that Karavelic had of knowing what his powers were and having a clear source of authority. That lack of sanctions is very important. We refer -- we refer you to our Defence final brief at paragraphs 363 to 367 inclusive. The Prosecution in their closing and their final brief gave you almost nothing on the question of effective control and how Halilovic himself exercised it and you look in vain for that. The Prosecution have listed a number of incidents and episodes. They are entitled, of course, to refer to the evidence and deal with it as they see fit. The reason they couldn't get specific about it is because whenever you do you keep coming up against the same reality: Halilovic could not command these people and expect them to obey because of the military structure. Your Honours, I turn to the ability of Halilovic to effectively control the 9th Brigade, soldiers, who went down to Herzegovina. In reality, the chain of command was broken. Even if Halilovic had have been appointed, even if he wanted to issue commands, the chain of command between him and the killers was broken. It was broken again and again at different points. He was unable to exercise that effective control. The Prosecutors argue this: There is a chain of command that goes from Sefer Halilovic here as commander, through Zulfikar Alispago, through Ramiz Delalic, Celo, to the killers. That's the chain that the Prosecution argue. Your Honours, that's broken at numerous points. I'll start with Zulfikar Alispago. I've already said something about that. I'm not going to repeat everything that we said that we rely on there. But you couldn't find the positive fact that Halilovic had effective control over Zulfikar Alispago. It's not proved. I've indicated Zulfikar was a person who refused resubordination, and I've pointed you to Exhibits P120 and D443 to prove that. Karavelic gave evidence on the 20th of April at pages 40 to 42 how Zulfikar Alispago during the battle at Igman simply got up and went home and left the battle zone. There is not an order in existence showing that Halilovic is ordering to Alispago nor is there evidence of Alispago obeying any order of Halilovic. Karic gave evidence of the tearing up. I've given these accounts already. You know about the combat order, D273, and you know about the reports by Zulfikar Alispago direct to Delic. And all of those matters tell against a conclusion that Halilovic could exercise or did exercise effective control over Zulfikar Alispago. Now, the next person over whom effective control couldn't be exercised was Ramiz Delalic, Celo. Now, this is a serious point and the Prosecution seem to have no way out of this dilemma. They needed to show that Delalic was an insubordinate person because they wanted to say that that was part of Halilovic knowing how bad and naughty the 9th Brigade were, so they pointed you to that in their brief. But I would ask you to look at paragraph 94 of the Prosecution final brief. Here you will find the express statement, paragraph 94: "The evidence established that by September 1993 the 9th Motorised Brigade and the 10th Motorised Brigade," and it sets out all these good things about those brigades. I'm not going to read them all . But the fourth point is this: "Largely operated outside the ABiH system of command and control." If you look at the last dot point in that list it says: "Attempts to bring these renegade brigades back into the system of command and control were unsuccessful until Operation Trebevic in October 1993." Now, that's the end. They are not in effective control. They are outside the line of command and control. The Prosecution did not plead or undertake to prove any alternative chain. The evidence wouldn't support it if they did plead that. You cannot both put a unit outside the system of command and control and seek to rely on command responsibility against Sefer Halilovic. It's not just a logical trick; it's the reality. It's -- it was the Defence case even before these concessions were made that you just couldn't control that. Now, apart from seeing it here in Court the evidence was - and we're going to take you to some of it - very clear about that individual, Ramiz Delalic, Celo. The Prosecution have simply said what was realistic. The 9th Brigade was outside the effective control of the army. That's what the Prosecutor says. "Largely operated outside the ABiH system of command and control." In that situation, they had to say there's some other way in which effective control could be exercised, but no such pleading, no such evidence. Let's go through why it is, apart from the Prosecution's -- what I submit is a clear concession. The Prosecution themselves referred at paragraphs 116, 118, and 124 to incidents which reveal the fact that Delalic simply did not obey orders unless it suited him to do so. In our brief there's a lengthy treatment of this, it's in paragraph 357. We just refer you to that. We don't have time to rehearse it and you don't need us to rehearse it. But we've dealt with this question specifically. I'll remind you of the 18th of April, that Vahid Karavelic at page 158 indicated the way to get Mr. Delalic to comply was to ask him nicely. He was always insubordinate. He was insubordinate before this action happened in September 1993. He was insubordinate during it, and he was insubordinate after it. Before it happened, the best example is that insurrection of the 2nd of July. It's a minor incident. It doesn't tell you that Ramiz Delalic was going to go and kill civilians or place civilians in any danger. It doesn't help the Prosecution from that point of view. What it shows is that he was outside the line of command and control. He didn't obey. When you get down to Herzegovina during the course of these operations, you only have to look at how he behaved in the famous incident at Zuka's flat to see whether he was prepared to obey orders or not. In that incident you'll remember that on the 10th, on the evening of the 10th of September, there was a meeting at Zulfikar Alispago's flat. It was attended by the investigators. There was Namik Dzankovic, his helper from the civilian authorities, a man named Brankovic. Also there was Salihamidzic from the local police station, and -- I just can't remember who else there was there but there was a couple of others. And Zulfikar Alispago, I'm sorry, of course, himself. And they were discussing the incidents that had happened and obviously discussing what was to be done when into that meeting came bursting two people, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and a large individual named Malco. And on that occasion, the evidence was simply -- well, it was unrefuted, that Ramiz Delalic said, Zuka, give me a car. I'm taking the units back to Sarajevo. What are you worried about a few dead Croats for? Words to that effect. I point out again the anomaly of Halilovic being in the dock and Ramiz Delalic being in the witness box. But for our purposed now I point out that Delalic was outside the system of command and control. What you have there -- and there was significant cross-examination and evidence in-chief about it from the Prosecutors, was a man who was not compliant with the system of command and control. He was the one giving the orders, and Zulfikar Alispago was the one who was begging and pleading and saying, Come on, don't be like that, and trying to persuade him it was a very good thing to save the people down in Mostar. Now, whatever inference you derive from that you cannot derive an inference that he was complicit and complying with the system of command and control. It's the complete reverse of that. And after the event you turn to the Trebevic operation on the 26th of October, when Ramiz Delalic, upon being lawfully dismissed, finally lawfully dismissed by the president, Ramiz Delalic commenced a siege at which he had 300 civilians and threatened to blow the lot of them up. Ended up negotiating some form of surrender after a day of exchanges of fire, all of which is the subject of evidence. Another proof of Ramiz Delalic not being in this line of command and control anticipates something I'll say when we get to the failure to punish the crime at Grabovica is that he actively blocked that investigation, and the evidence was quite clear about that. On the afternoon of the 9th he met with Sead Kurt, the military policeman on the iron bridge while Salihamidzic was down on the water looking for bodies, and he expressed a hostility at that time towards the investigation. At Zuka's flat he expressed hostility towards the investigation. D226 is -- sorry, I didn't note the tab number of that. It's behind tab number 17, Your Honours. Is a report from Nermin Eminovic concerning the situation in the village of Grabovica at the time of that report. And in that report, Eminovic refers in the last few lines of that report to the prospect of revolt by the units and return to Sarajevo. We'll demonstrate that later on what that all means and why that made it very dangerous and difficult to go into the village and do anything there. But right now it's relevant to effective control. Effective control does not include a state of revolt or rebellion. That was the state Ramiz Delalic was in: He obeyed when he wanted to obey. He was not under anyone's effective control. Zulfikar Alispago did not have effective control over Delalic. You can see that from the incident at the flat. And the fact that Celo's men or some of them fought in the battle is not a meaningful indicator that they were compliant. And the reason for that is that you could fight in that battle under Alispago without being subordinated. Look at the 2nd Independent Battalion. Exhibit D270 is that chronological report. It was tendered through Witness Okovic. And in that report and in evidence Okovic made it quite clear that the 2nd Independent Battalion refused to be resubordinated to the Zulfikar unit, simply refused. Nevertheless, they still fought. And this I think is an illustration of what my learned friend Ms. Chana described as an army that didn't operate by the book. They operated on a basis of agreements, persuading. It's not effective control in those circumstances. Your Honours, I should correct something. I have to put this on the record here. At page 24, line 2, I mentioned an exhibit which was an order, purported order of Halilovic, which is not really an order of Halilovic at all. I said it was P121. It's really P122, that document, and I won't go back over it now for time reasons. But it's the order -- it's got Halilovic's name written under it, but in fact when you look at it it's a draft and it's been written in -- or proposed, it's been written in Jablanica and sent to Halilovic personally among others, up in Sarajevo. But you can draw this conclusion very simply: Ramiz Delalic, Celo, did not obey Zulfikar Alispago, Zuka. Did not obey. That's the evidence, and there's none the other way. For that reason, the Prosecution felt compelled to lead evidence of a special relationship. The Prosecution indicated that they called Ramiz Delalic here because Sefer took him to Herzegovina. Well, the reason they really called him is to try and prove some sort of special relationship between the two of them. Now, Your Honours, what we submit is the evidence of Ramiz Delalic did not, even if you believed it, even if you accepted a word of it, and I'll tell you in a minute why that should not happen, but even if you believed that it did not amount to effective control, all it amounted to was a preference on behalf of Ramiz Delalic for Sefer Halilovic in comparison to Mr. Delic. Delalic made it quite clear in his own mind that most of the brigade commanders were of the same view, or the majority of brigade commanders were of the same view. Now, Your Honours, the truth is that you cannot believe anything said by Ramiz Delalic. It's not a question of believing one part and dismissing other parts. He's a witness who should be rejected in total because he's got a position to protect. And he came here to tell an integrated story. His whole story was designed to protect him from liability for what he plainly did wrong in Grabovica, namely, to block the investigation and shield his own forces, who he must have known, some of whom he must have known were involved in crimes. Delalic, in our submission, is a liar, a person who was proved to be a liar. The Prosecution has tacitly accepted that position because in their brief they do not rely nor in oral submissions do they rely on the most outrageous claim that he made. You will remember that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, came to this Court and said that Halilovic and Zulfikar Alispago actively covered up the crime at Grabovica and included in that theory of his was that they proposed the removal and at least at one point in his evidence the killing of those boys. That was his theory. Now, if that's true, it's very important evidence against Halilovic. But it's not true. It's obviously a load of lies, and we can demonstrate that because it conflicts with just about everything else. The Prosecution didn't persist with that argument. They know it's not true. They're not troubling you with determining that matter, and you don't have to determine it because they haven't argued it, and we have to keep this matter confined to the issues between the parties. But what I'm putting to you here is that the Prosecution don't hold out Ramiz Delalic as a truthful person. They say he disposed of the bodies. Indictment, paragraph 20, makes that explicit. The Prosecution persisted from the beginning in not telling me, or you, the Tribunal, which parts of that evidence they relied upon and which parts they don't rely on. They were asked many times; they didn't say. Your Honours, in our submission, he is not a witness who you could rely on on any view of things at all. Let me just take you to a couple of quick issues about that, but really, we can't distract into why Ramiz Delalic is a difficult person to accept. We say that he is a criminal, a bad one; we say he is a manipulator of the court processes; we say that he colluded with other witnesses, notably Witness D. You might remember Witness D did say here at one point that he knew that somebody was bringing a particular document to give evidence later in the case, which could only have been Delalic; we say he's got an association with the investigation through the investigator Mikhailov where he provided and procured witnesses; we say he has told revealed and clear lies about his role; his trip to Jablanica, which he denies in evidence, was proved to have happened by witnesses, even witnesses friendly to him. His trip to Grabovica was proved. He went to Grabovica. His alibi was a very -- well, it's a matter for you to decide whether it's convincing or not. He's had many changes of story which were put to him in evidence. And he made a claim about Halilovic and Zulfikar Alispago and Karic in the middle of the afternoon of the 9th, which the Prosecution have simply disregarded, and rightly disregarded. Your Honours, you can reject his claims about a special relationship, and if you reject those claims there's nothing left of the special relationship argument because the operative information, those many featherweight documents of gossip from the security services cannot be relied on for the truth of their content. They can establish the fact that the security services were collecting information, but they can't establish the truth of what's in them. You, as professional Judges, are the best people in the world to assess the weight of those individual documents, but they're all feathers. Ten of them weigh no more than one of them. They'll all lightweight documents, and they don't prove the truth of their contents. And nor do we expect the Prosecutor to rely on them heavily, but that's a matter for the Prosecutors, of course, and determinative for you. Anyway, that's why we say that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, ought not be believed. And that's why we say that you could not accept that he was a person who was in effective control of anyone. And if you were not prepared to take the step that you're invited to take by me at this moment, which is to say that man was out of control and is not capable of being effectively controlled, then at the very least you can build it into all the other things to estimate whether or not Halilovic had effective control of Ramiz Delalic. Because as well as Halilovic being a lame duck, and as well as the Bosnian army not having enforcement mechanisms, Ramiz Delalic was a man who simply did not comply. Now, all of that adds up to this, in my submission, that Halilovic was not in much of a position -- not in a position to exercise effective control. The resubordination orders, if you accepted them, are just orders. They don't indicate effective control; they just indicate the wishes of commanders at various points. And I want to make this point clear, too. My learned friend Mr. Mettraux will expand on it legally, but you have to draw a distinction between effective control and influence. Even if Halilovic were established to have some level of influence, even if it was a strong level of influence, that is not effective control. Now I'll just mention at the end of that section this: The standard of proof is beyond reasonable doubt. The Prosecution have got to show to beyond reasonable doubt that Halilovic was in effective control of Ramiz Delalic. On the face of what I've put there, Your Honours, it seems, in my -- well, I submit that it's established that he was not, but at least we say that we've raised a doubt about the matter which you can never get rid of. Effective control of the Prozor Independent Battalion is a different matter. There you have a clear situation where Halilovic does not have command power and -- although the structure of orders allowed the Prosecution to mount an argument as to de jure control over Ramiz Delalic, the position is absolutely crystal clear with respect to the Prozor Independent Battalion de jure, that battalion remained in the 6th Corps. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence that Halilovic had command authority over the 6th Corps and Gusic, there is a de jure block to effective control. But when you combine that with the way Buza -- Commander Buza behaved himself towards Halilovic, it becomes clear that there were grave limits on Halilovic's ability in that regard, too. Buza displayed an attitude of animosity. I'm quoting here Witness J. Witness J was asked questions by Your Honour Judge El Mahdi about this. He indicated that Buza displayed animosity. When Your Honour asked whether or not -- what effect that had on Halilovic's power and whether he had clout, Witness J said: "He had no practical power at all." That's uncontradicted evidence in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe it's too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honours, could I just invite you, in a slow and measured tone, to regard the evidence of Witness J as persuasive, sensible, considered evidence from a good person, educated, honest, and not amenable to criticism. Since he's not contradicted, you can act on his evidence. Since no one contradicted him. One of the great things about Witness J was that he was not racially prejudiced. He made it quite clear that he was grateful for the help he got from his Croatian friends, and there is no basis for disbelieving him. He was found by the Defence. He gave his evidence here. That's the sort of evidence you need in this Court. You don't need to hear Ramiz Delalic telling you lies and malicious lies. You need to hear the witnesses who tell the truth. Now, Your Honours, other indications about Commander Buza was that he did not go into battle on the 13th when he should have gone into battle. Now, the Prosecution's case is that Halilovic was the commander. If Halilovic was the commander, Buza's failure to go into battle is a serious indicator of whether Halilovic had effective control over him or not. Buza was not sanctioned for this act. Can you imagine the situation in any other army if somebody simply didn't go into battle and caused that part of the operation to be seriously compromised? But the evidence is that Buza was promoted; he was not sacked. I just remind the Court to consider if you were satisfied that Halilovic had effective control over Buza, it's a very short time period that he had it because he left the area on the 15th, the inspection team wound up on the 20th, there's a cease-fire which was not effective down in the Vrdi area, the area where Celo's soldiers were and is not relevant to that part of the proceedings, but that cease-fire may also be a convenient point at which to say that Halilovic's relationship with the Prozor Independent Battalion ended. So that has an impact at a later stage, if you found he was in effective control as to how long he had to do anything about it. Your Honours, that brings to an end the effective control segment. It's a matter of -- the Prosecution have to prove beyond reasonable doubt. We submit for all of those reasons that they can't do so. Now, Your Honours, I want to move to another topic. And we move now to the knowledge and notice of the accused in relation to the crime of murder and the mode of that crime being the failure to prevent the crime at Grabovica. And in considering this, you need to consider how the Prosecution prove its case. I've already been through the elements that the Prosecution have to prove. There are two ways of proving the notice of Halilovic. The Prosecution prove that he had actual knowledge, which is what the indictment set out to do. Or, in theory, the Prosecution can prove constructive knowledge. Now, Your Honours, we have to meet three different cases on this topic. We say we meet them all easily. We say, also, as an initial point that we shouldn't have to meet three, we should have to meet one; but so as not to be stranded and sitting on a high horse protesting about it we're going to meet the cases as best we can. Your Honours, the first case of the Prosecution in this regard is that which is pleaded in the indictment at paragraph 15 and in the pre-trial brief at paragraphs 95 to 98. This was an actual knowledge case. It was said there that Halilovic really did learn of the killings while they were going on, and it was said that he was in Jablanica, he was told about it. And it was then said, and it was completely intellectually coherent and sensible to say at the point when he got that actual knowledge, there and then, he had duties. Duties arose for him at that point. That's a coherent way to argue. It's a sensible way to argue. Once the knowledge is proved, and at the point the knowledge is proved, then, and only then, do the duties arise. So once Halilovic found out about the crimes happening, he had to go and take certain action. And there can be argument as to whether the Prosecutor had properly pleaded the actions that he should take. But that was the case. Now, that case did not materialise in evidence. The Prosecution did not prove or lead any evidence that's capable of proving that case. When you come to consider actual knowledge, therefore, the verdict must be not guilty. It has to be, because the Prosecution -- even if you believe their witnesses, drew all the bad inferences, you'll be left with this: That Halilovic didn't find out until after it was finished. So he didn't have actual knowledge. That's the case the Prosecution pleaded and that's the one that they failed to prove. And I'm not going to spend any more time on it because the Prosecution didn't seek to persist with it. But another case emerged that the Prosecution wished to persist with, and that was a case that arose out of, what is known as, in this case as being known as the Karic incident. That's the incident where it is alleged by the friends of Ramiz Delalic, not by others but by them, that Karic made an inappropriate comment. That's the claim made by those witnesses, who we say are bad witnesses. Now, the Prosecution at that time in constructing that case have pleadings problems. We've referred to those in our brief. I'm not going to reiterate them now. I'm going to deal with it if you allow them to argue that. The Prosecution there said that Halilovic should have responded. Once he heard that comment, that he then had duties and he should have responded. Now, it's very doubtful, Your Honours, whether the notice that Halilovic had, even if that comment was true, was sufficient for 7(3) liability. Because what has to be proved is that there was a substantial likelihood that the crime of murder about to occur. But the Defence to this charge is really much simpler than that. We just say it's not proved that that happened. It's not proved -- first of all, it's not proved that Karic said that. That Karic incident, we say, is a fabrication, a nasty fabrication.
