And we say that the Prosecution have not proved beyond a reasonable doubt nor have they tried to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Karic did say it. Karic himself denies saying such a thing. He denies it. He was a witness of good character, not self-serving. There were many reasons why he would not say such a thing. He was obviously part of a coordination of combat activities. On the Prosecution's case he's a part of a team that's commanding them. And his own son was there, and his son is half Croatian and his son has Croatian grandparents. And to cut a long story short, it takes a lot of believing that he would say such a comment and he denies it. So that's a powerful matter to weigh. Secondly, the people who accuse him of saying such a thing are all of them friends with each other, all of them friends with Ramiz Delalic, and all of them tainted by a stain of collusion which we submit you might decide was proved absolutely clearly, not just because of the way their stories changed but because of what happened over the course of the hearings here. The Prosecution led that evidence from those witnesses but no other witnesses said that that happened. According to the three accusers, the three friends of Celo effectively, many, many other soldiers were there. All of them, in fact, were called by commanders and lined up. But that's not what the other witnesses said: Sakrak, Kadic. So you would expect corroboration. If that was the story, you would expect corroboration. For such an outrageous comment, you would expect lots of corroboration, but there's none, and those three can't corroborate each other because they're colluding together. Of course they say the same thing. The Prosecution themselves, perfectly reasonably, recognised a reasonable doubt. I'm just going to read out paragraph 102 -- sorry, 201 from their brief. Paragraph 201 says this: "Karic, as one would expect, denies telling the soldiers that they should throw villagers in the river or kill them. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from which it could make a positive finding that Karic gave the soldiers the green light to harm or even kill the civilians. The Prosecution notes that Karic would be very unlikely to admit making this remark, but also notes that the murders were committed by members of Arnautovic and Witness D's unit, and both could have been attempting to shift the blame on to Karic for what occurred. The Trial Chamber does not have to make positive findings one way or the other about this allegation to proceed to convict Sefer Halilovic." We'll deal with that last allegation a bit later on. But the Prosecution in that paragraph are, in my submission, clearly conceding that there is a reasonable doubt that Karic made this comment. And whether you regard them as making that concession formally or not, I do not mind. It's just common sense. There's a reasonable doubt that that happened. The Prosecution themselves seem to recognise that, but you as professional Judges would, in my submission, recognise it without any trouble because Karic was a good witness. I just want to point out some, if you like, characteristics of this false story against Karic. We constructed in our brief at paragraph 451 a chronology, and the reason why that was done at such length was so that you could measure the claims of these three individuals against that chronology. The chronology's constructed from the victims, from Salihamidzic, from people who are reliable, sensible witnesses and -- anyway, it's an accountable chronology. You can look at it and see whether you think it's valid or not. We urge you to follow it and make findings that that chronology is right. But the uncontroversial steps in it are these: The troops did arrive on the 8th of September; Karic and Dzankovic did visit the troops in the afternoon on the 8th of September; Pero Maric was killed that night; killings did proceed over the course of that night, the 8th and 9th; the murders at Witness A's house took place at some stage in the morning of the 9th; Salihamidzic and Sead Kurt, the local policeman and the military policeman, went to the village around 3.00, maybe a little bit later, and were there for some time on the 9th; the boys were kept overnight in that village by Ramiz Delalic, and on the morning of the 10th they boys went and were handed over to Zulfikar Alispago. And that account is borne out by the boys or by Witness A's own account by the contemporaneous statement, which was Exhibit 421, tendered, you'll remember they made a statement that was taken by Zulfikar's soldiers. They weren't covering up. The statement was taken by Zulfikar's soldiers at that time. So that's the chronology. And that's uncontroversial. When you measure against that what was said by these three individuals who accuse Karic, they all give the same false story. Now, people can get the right story the same because it's the truth, and people can make mistakes and get the wrong story in a variety of different ways. But as professional Judges when you see three people who are very suspicious in any event telling the same wrong story, the conclusion begins to look like it could be that they are colluding together. And when you then look at them and see that they are all friends with Ramiz Delalic and have all had contact with him since the war, that smell of collusion gets even stronger. Witness D, you'll recall this matter, there was a connection it didn't reflect on Witness D criminally himself, but there was a connection in an indictment. The same went for Witness Mehanovic. Witness Arnautovic told you that Ramiz Delalic was one of the best people you could know. When it came to what happened in that hotel, you didn't have a clear admission from any of them that they were colluding, but the evidence just established beyond a shadow of a doubt that they were discussing the case and you just shouldn't rely on their evidence. But, Your Honours, we're arguing about something that's the first line of defence way out there. What really the Prosecutor needed to prove was that Halilovic was part of this discussion and that he heard, and for that proposition there's one witness, and that's Witness D. Now, the reasons you disbelieve him are as follows: Karic and Dzankovic both say that Halilovic wasn't there. And whatever they might say about Karic, Dzankovic is a good, sensible, honest witness called by them in that capacity. No purpose to serve, no purpose to undermine him. He says Halilovic wasn't there, and in my submission you might well believe that and should believe it. Secondly, it seems likely that Halilovic was up in the Konjic area. There's evidence from Hodzic, Okovic, and Halilovic's own comments in his book which make that likely and suggest that that's what happened. Thirdly, there are other people who didn't see Halilovic there. Enes Sakrak gave evidence that he was sitting around in the house with Pero Maric while he was still alive, and there was no line-up of the kind described by these three individuals. Witness D himself, we submit, that he was really quite a dreadful witness. We ask you to look at paragraph 458 of the Defence brief to deal with that, but just like with the three of them he's particularly bad. He's got a link to Delalic. There's the collusion issue, there's the motivation to protect Ramiz Delalic, he has numerous changes of story, he made what is clearly a false allegation against Zulfikar Alispago. His own role was a little bit sinister. The Defence cannot make wild allegations based on the evidence and his denials of the proposition. I am not in a position to put to you and I don't put to you now that he's one of the killers. He was questioned about it. The proposition was put to him. He denied it. We deal in evidence in this Court, and you can't find that he was a killer. But he shares lies with the others in a sinister way, and his story of not hearing things on the night of the 8th is just not believable or acceptable. The Prosecution didn't believe it when it came from Mr. Arnautovic, and the same logic has got to apply to Witness D. Your Honours should find this: The Karic incident didn't occur, and it's a load of lies and it shouldn't have been led in this Court. If you're left in doubt about that, you couldn't, in my submission, find that Halilovic was present or that he overheard it or knew about it or had anything to do with it or was put on notice by it. That case is dead and finished and we invite you to so rule, if you feel that you have to rule on it because it's not in the indictment. So this left the Prosecution in significant trouble, but however never give up. When you look at the indictment you'll see that amongst the background facts the Prosecution pleaded about -- there was an actual knowledge case that I've already talked about with you. The Prosecution said that partially based upon his previous knowledge of the notorious reputation of the 9th Brigade, I think 10th Brigade as well, Halilovic upon learning of the actual killings going on was then duty-bound to act. The knowledge of the reputation of the 9th Brigade and so on was in those days merely a background fact, nothing more than that. However, in opening this case my learned friend Ms. Chana on page 31 of the indictment said -- I'm sorry, I read that wrong. The transcript. The transcript of the 31st of January on page 19. My learned friend Ms. Chana said: "Given that the accused had knowledge of the criminal propensity of these two brigades, he was necessarily aware of the likelihood that they might commit crimes in Grabovica." Now, this is a new case. We say it's a recent invention of a case. We say that's got pleadings implications but we've argued that in the brief and we don't want to waste time in repeating that now. But we'll deal with the substance of it. We say it's a recent invention by the Prosecution which reveals the weakness of their case. It was intellectually adept, and we don't -- it's not a question of saying the Prosecution are silly or evil in some way. They're constructing a case, but you're entitled to assess it coldly as Judges. We say that that argument was always very inadequate in law because it ignores certain needs that the Prosecution have to meet. It ignores the danger the accused is supposed to be on notice of was a danger of crimes of murder. It ignores that the danger has to be of a substantial likelihood. It ignores that the danger had to be immediate, or to quote,"about to be committed." Therefore, the possibility of a crime is not enough. Substantial likelihood of some other kind of a crime is not enough, and a floating sense of danger that they might commit a crime one day or at some stage is not enough. And this allegation of the Prosecutors is just too remote to allow the notice component to be established. It ignores some basic facts, and then at a later stage I'm going to say to you even apart from ignoring those facts the substance of it doesn't stand up. But the basic facts it ignores are: First of all, that Halilovic did not select the troops himself. It's evident that there was discussion preceding the choosing of those troops. D406 is behind tab 333. We don't need to go to that; you already have. But that's the one that showed that the inspection team was discussing with Commander Delic before Sefer Halilovic even arrived in Herzegovina the provision of troops. What you know is that when the troops actually did leave, present at that departure was Vahid Karavelic who you might think -- the Prosecution said he was an charismatic, excellent witness, and all praise to him. Well, the Defence's position is a bit more moderate about him. We simply say he was a good officer doing his job. But he was present when they left. So too was Ramiz Delalic. An MP, Sarcirovic [phoen], the official commander of the 9th Brigade was also present. The order of Halilovic pursuant to which Karavelic did his job is P161; it's behind tab 13. We've spent some time on that, but what I'm going to say now is something about the substance of that order. Look and see what Halilovic actually did. He provided a range of units from whom Karavelic was to select troops. It is not accurate to say Halilovic chose the troops. He didn't choose the troops. He simply provided, if you like, a deck of cards for others to select the troops from. The second reality that's a very important one that the current Prosecution case, being constructed as it is, can't meet is this one: That it wasn't Halilovic who had the role of billeting those troops. It was Vehbija Karic. Now, Karic -- the Defence says Karic did everything right. We're going to justify what Karic did. We don't really have to do that because I'm not defending Mr. Karic; I'm defending Mr. Halilovic. But we want to do that to show that the Prosecution's case is an artificial one. It's an attempt to put together duties and obligations and failures from a case that really fell in ruins when they found that the evidence about the 8th of September was inadequate. What Karic did was that he did go and inspect the scene first. He spoke to the villagers. Karic's own account is that he secured the agreement of villagers. Karic was an experienced officer. I interplay this: That Halilovic would have been well entitled to believe that the billeting of the troops was in good hands. And in fact you might come to the same view. You can't allow hindsight to turn these men into monsters. They at the time acted in good faith. Halilovic went to the village -- sorry, Karic went to the village and looked. He got agreement. He decided to billet the troops there. When they were there, Karic and Dzankovic went to visit them. Now, the Prosecution relied on a comment made by Jusuf Jasarevic that there should have been a security assessment done. Now, no format for doing that was explained in court, and in the realities of the Bosnian situation, my learned friend Ms. Chana said that we're not playing things by the book here. But if a security assessment was needed both before and after the troops arrived, it happened. It happened with senior officers and the security officer of the inspection team going there to inspect, and what they saw was very encouraging. I'll say something about why the village was a good village to select. That's in our brief, of course. But that village had a history of nice, welcoming, kindly people, Bosnian citizens of Croat ethnicity who were nice to the citizens. They were good to the soldiers. There was a good relationship between Zulfikar Alispago and those people. Jablanica was in a mess; Grabovica was peaceful. Karic made, according to what he knew and the information he had, the right choice in billeting those troops where he did. Karic didn't deny it. Karic said in evidence that he didn't believe Halilovic even knew that Grabovica was chosen as the place. There's no evidence that suggests or that counters what Karic says about that. You can't infer it from what Halilovic did in the days before. Prosecution proved a couple of visits by Halilovic to Grabovica, but on neither occasion could it be said that there was a decision taken to put these troops in Grabovica. On the 1st of the 9th, when Halilovic went there, he went to the left bank with Hodzic and other people, but on that occasion the 9th Brigade hadn't been chosen. There was no question of billeting them. On the 3rd of September Halilovic went there again, this time in a car with Zulfikar with Alispago and Sevko Hodzic, but on that occasion they didn't even stop at Grabovica. And the Prosecution did not prove, and it's not because they're slow or silly, it's because they know what the evidence is. They didn't prove that Halilovic knew that there was about to be a billeting of these troops in Grabovica. You see, the knowledge has got to arise at a fixed point. The Prosecution's got to prove: This is the moment he realised and that's when his duties arose. And that's when he should have fixed in his mind that there was a substantial likelihood of crimes about to happen, crimes of murder about to happen. So the Defence says that it was fatally flawed, the concept of this -- of knowing about the troops being bad, even if he knew they were monsters, it was never able to weep, it was never able to get a conviction on what was pleaded. They had to prove that at some stage Halilovic knew it was going to happen, and they didn't really try to prove it, but in any event we say that they certainly didn't succeed. That brings me to the substance of the argument, Your Honour. When I say "substance," it brings me to the Prosecution's own battleground, that even if you allowed that it was possible to have this sort of floating knowledge putting you on notice, the Defence says that what was known to Halilovic about the 9th Brigade just was not that bad, just didn't put him on notice that crimes of murder were likely or even possible. The evidence proved that the 9th Brigade soldiers were mostly good people. The evidence is, I'm not going to go into specifics about this, there's plenty of evidence, it's in our brief, but the evidence supported that it was a multi-ethnic unit. The evidence supported that it was -- did not have a history of ethnic strife. The evidence supported that it did not have a history of murder. The Prosecution sought to blur that with what was known about the 10th Brigade, but the 10th Brigade didn't commit the killings. We do not accept that the bad and extreme crimes alleged against the 10th Brigade were known to Halilovic at all. But we ask you not to get distracted by what the 10th Brigade did and what Halilovic knew about the 10th Brigade. They're not the killers. And it's the killers in respect of whom the duties arose, not other people. The problems that the Prosecution pointed to concerning the 9th Brigade were, in my submission, minor matters once they were analysed properly. The digging of trenches does not put anyone on notice of the likelihood of murders. Trenches -- the misdemeanours or disciplinary breaches constituted by taking people away to dig trenches involved an organised activity for the purposes of defence of Sarajevo; it wasn't criminality in the usual self-serving or rebellious nature. It was directly related to the needs of saving the town. It was organised. The Prosecution have claimed that they exposed people to danger. Anyone who has any familiarity -- reading this brief and hearing the evidence in this case, there was no safe place in Sarajevo at that time. But in any event, you've heard from a person who was taken to the front line and he gave you what you might think was a very philosophical and sensible approach to what happened and why it was done. The trench-digging, however you characterise it, we're not inviting you to put a stamp on approval upon the illegal taking of people away to dig trenches. We don't ask you to do that. But you shouldn't make a finding that units who take people away to dig trenches are likely to commit random, pointless killings of people, lovely people, old people. That inference isn't open. Now, the next matter that the Prosecution raised against the 9th Brigade was that they were collecting or there was some collection of contributions from local businessmen. They colourfully described that it was extortion. Perhaps it's extortion, but that doesn't tell you that they're going to take murderous action against poor, old civilians. The. Prosecution also relied on smuggling, but the evidence about that from Karavelic was that it was just a reality. Ramiz Delalic smuggled food and weapons for his units. That wasn't proved to have any criminal intent at all. It was illegal use of the tunnel and gaining weapons but whatever means were available to him to do. You've heard evidence about that. It was one of the great problems of the Prosecution case that they call Ramiz Delalic, meaning from the beginning to call him a liar at all times. Your Honours, they put a number of specific allegations against the 9th Brigade at paragraphs 95 right through until paragraph -- well, there's quite a number of paragraphs there, up to paragraph 126 covers a lot of them. They list things that the 9th Brigade did wrong. Now, what we'd say about those is that the criminal behaviour was minor, the insubordination behaviour was serious, but the insubordination doesn't tell you there's going to be killings in Grabovica or anywhere else. They didn't kill people. The proof is in the pudding. The Prosecution didn't prove a single murder committed by members of the 9th Brigade. And sensible witnesses, such as Witness Kemal Kapur, who is a judge now, who was a member of the 9th Brigade told you that most of them were okay. They were good people to choose, generally speaking. And what we would point out is it was a skillful rhetorical device when Mr. Weiner blurred together in submissions the activities of the 9th Brigade and the 10th Brigade. He's just doing his job. It's my job to point it out. And I do point it out that there is a difference between what was known about the 9th and what was known about the 10th. Your Honours, that's what the 9th Brigade actually did. The next question is: What did Halilovic know about it? The Prosecution gave you many operative documents. We don't have time to go through those documents in detail of course, but I urge you to look at them individually and see whether any of them had to be shown to Halilovic, and the answer will be very few. Most of those documents are internal working documents of one of the two security services, the state security services, the SJB. They are the units that had Halilovic under surveillance. Because from June onwards he was under surveillance. So it's very unlikely that those documents were shared with Halilovic in any form. Now, the Prosecution in an attempt to attribute to Halilovic knowledge of the more florid activities of the 10th Brigade simply led a list of meetings that Halilovic might have attended and opportunities for him to hear certain information. But this matter has to be dealt with as strict proof. The Prosecution did not prove that Halilovic had knowledge of any murderous tendencies on the part of 9th Brigade or any of its soldiers. The Prosecution proved that Halilovic must have known about the trench-digging. Of course he knew about that. And although it's not directly proved that he knew about any specific incidents, it's likely, too, that he would have known about some illegal activities by some members. It's very unlikely that he would have known about it in detail or as to the specific people, who they were. He's operating at a high level of generality. He was in command of the army most of the time, and then after that he was the Chief of Staff. So what he had to know and what he was likely to know is general information. But the Prosecution did not prove that he knew about murders. And in fact they didn't prove that there were any murders, but there's a throw-away reference to the 10th Brigade's involvement at Kazani. But we'd ask you to find specifically that Halilovic didn't know about that. No one suggested that he did and no one is suggesting an opportunity when he would. Your Honours, therefore, the notice of Halilovic was very mild. He knew the 9th Brigade was a unit that had problems of insubordination and he knew that about the commander, Ramiz Delalic, but he didn't know that the troops were an evil group, and the truth is they weren't. And the conclusion from that is knowing what he knew about that unit, he had no basis for concluding, just like everyone else had no basis for concluding, that innocent, old civilians would be slaughtered by members of that unit. Your Honour, the measures which were appropriate for Halilovic to take according to the Prosecutor are artificial. Now, you'll see they invent new ones daily because after we got the Prosecution final brief, in argument yesterday a new one came along. And yesterday it was said that Halilovic should have provided criteria for selection of troops. Now, that's not in the indictment, in the brief, it wasn't in the opening, and it wasn't in their final brief. It's not realistic to suggest that Halilovic order -- guessing how the ingenious minds of the Prosecutors work. The Prosecutors are thinking on their feet, imaginatively intelligently, trained lawyers. And they've got no idea what the duties are. They make them up as they go along and they put them to the Court in the construction of the case, but never did they identify at any time a sensible, coherent body of obligations on Halilovic, nor did they identify when those obligations arise. And it will be interesting to see, Your Honours, when the time for reply comes, whether the Prosecution then seek to advance a time and wait and see whether they do or they don't a time at which this duty was imposed on Halilovic. They haven't done it up to now, and we'll see when it is they do with an hour to go in the trial. So, Your Honours, the duties that they listed, we say, are to be dismissed. The first duty they suggest was at paragraph 252 and following. They said: "There should have been care in the selection of units." Your Honours, we point out in response to that one that there has to be a personal dereliction by Halilovic. Halilovic merely asked-- merely instructed and ordered by P161 Karavelic to send certain troops, and he left the actual selection of those troops to Karavelic, who did so obviously by consulting people lower down the scale. And in fact the individual choice may have been -- probably was done at a much lower level. Halilovic merely named the 9th as one of the sources from which these troops could be taken. And you'll see there there is flexible in that because Halilovic mentioned the Delta brigade in that order, but no Delta Brigade soldiers went. Your Honours, Karavelic himself said that he might have chosen those troops himself. Your Honour Judge El Mahdi asked him on the 22nd of April a question, and I just direct the Tribunal to the answers at page 161 concerning that. Jusuf Jasarevic indicated that he wouldn't have chosen those troops, but he also said that he would not foresee this, what happened, coming. Jasarevic also agreed -- sorry, Jasarevic said that on the 4th of March at page 61 and 62. The Prosecution of course didn't prove that there were any other troops available to take. A witness called Tirak suggested the 4th Brigade could, but he didn't know, and he admitted he didn't know whether they were available. In any event, you now know the 4th Brigade was Prevljak's brigade which was the obstructing brigade that didn't hand over the trucks. The next duty the Prosecution said was to warn the troops on their arrival of various duties. I think -- and I don't have a proper note of it, but I think the Prosecution's point was that they should be told of their obligations under international law. Your Honours, they were warned on departure by Karavelic as a responsible, sensible, perhaps even charismatic commander. And the question -- he was asked this at -- the 22nd of April - and I realise I'm going fast again, Your Honours - "when you spoke to these troops, I understand you may not recall the exact words that you used to them but I suppose you said in words that they -- well, I ask you this: In general terms, did you say in words that they could understand: Boys, fight well, don't hurt the civilians, and behave properly while you're down there? "A. I suppose that every single word you've just uttered must certainly be a part of that five-minute address on my part." They were warned. They're not obliged to have the Geneva Convention read out to them. It's got to be in language they understand. It's got to be sensible: Don't hurt the civilians. That's what Karavelic did. The Prosecution's allegation there just simply reflects that they didn't re-read the brief before they thought up that obligation because it was fulfilled by Karavelic. Your Honours, it was then said that there should have been a security assessment performed on arrival. Well, we say that Karic did that himself. It was then said that Halilovic failed to recognise the dangers. Well, in one sense that's quite true. Everyone failed to recognise the dangers. But no one's required to be clairvoyant, no one can see the future, no one foresaw the dangers. The Prosecution said this is not just hindsight when they referred to something said by Jasarevic that it was stupid to billet them. Well, it was hindsight. It was hindsight. He was here in evidence -- in court saying it was stupid. And it colours everything that you know what happened afterwards. But you can't be like that. You have to look at it from the standpoint of those who were billeting the troops. These were good boys with a decent reputation. It wasn't suggested that the bad people had been selected. It was then said that there was a failure to prepare a plan for the safety of villagers. Once again, we're dealing with Karic's obligations here. It was Karic who had the specific duty. The failure to assign military police was said to be one of these duties. Well, the first military police that the Prosecutors wanted to assign was the 9th Brigade. If you look at paragraph 97 of their brief, it would seem that the military police in that brigade were just as bad. Perhaps they were the worst. It's part of the Prosecution's case that evil individuals posing as military police from the 9th Brigade were committing the crimes in -- or the offences that -- the misdemeanours in Sarajevo itself. Then the Prosecution said that the 6th Corps military police order would have been used. There was no evidence at all that such troops were available on that day. There was a very misleading footnote in the Prosecution's brief. It's footnote 549. It refers to the 6th Corps military police, and the quote is: "Which had offered to assist Namik Dzankovic in Grabovica if help was needed." Because it's referring to the need to billet troops, that footnote, I'd ask you to have a look at that, that footnote suggests the offer already happened and Dzankovic already had in his hand the offer of military police. But in fact that offer was made after the killings had already happened on the 10th. So that footnote there, it must have just been an accident that it came out the way it did. We'd ask you to disregard that because it's post facto offer of military police. There was a failure according to the Prosecutors to evacuate, separate or plan or proportion -- take plans or precautions. Again, Karic did what he saw as necessary. Halilovic wasn't there. Karic did what was right. Failure to provide proper supervision. Well, Karic went to visit. We've taken the trouble to answer step by step by step here because we want to say that it's artificial. This case can never win. Even if you accepted everything the Prosecution said, which we say you shouldn't, it can never win. The Prosecution said about Halilovic's failure to respond to the supposed comments of Karic, "the Prosecution does not rely on this particular failure," page 74. The fact of the matter is this, Your Honour: That didn't happen. We ask you to make that finding specifically. Karic's reputation has been torn to pieces by three malignant liars in this court. And although you don't make findings to tear his reputation to pieces for the sheer sake of it, that man at significant personal cost to himself came and gave evidence, despite illness. I'm about to turn to the -- would you just excuse me one moment. Your Honours, if it's an appropriate time to take a break, I'm about to move to the failure to punish Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, I'm entirely in your hands. But at the same time I have to remind you that there's not so much time left on your part. So during the break I really hope the Defence team could streamline their presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just inquire. I have lost track of time. Could I inquire of the court staff what the remaining quota is -- sorry, we can do that in the break. I don't have to do that live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 30-minute break, and we will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, during the break I was reminded by the Court Deputy that Defence has 81 minutes left. And we could sit to quarter to 2.00, and we'll resume this afternoon at quarter past 3.00 for any rebuttal evidence or arguments, if the parties would like to present. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We move now to the crime -- the mode of murder, failing to punish Grabovica. Your Honours, it's nice to announce here that the Prosecution and Defence do not seem to be in dispute in any meaningful way, that notice and - by which I mean actual, real notice - of these crimes was proved by the evidence to exist in the evening, late afternoon, it's not important exactly when, but on the 9th of September. The evidence appears to support this, that at some time after 6.00 and before 9.00, Halilovic communicated to the journalist Sevko Hodzic that he had some knowledge, it's not clear what -- they were unable to talk because soldiers were around. So by that time it can be inferred that he knew something. It's not clear exactly what he knew. Later on that evening it was clear that he was aware of killings and we don't dispute what the Prosecutor said about that, that they knew enough to know that it could well have been military people. He doesn't need to know much more than that. And the exact degree of what he knew or suspected is not proved in evidence, but we accept that he had actual knowledge on the evening of the 9th of September. And he had knowledge of murders. So there's no dispute about all the of that. Now, Your Honours, we point out this that in terms of notice and in terms of his moral capability, what he did in response we say was appropriate. Halilovic's response was to express outrage to Namik Dzankovic to make it clear that he morally disapproved of what happened and he distanced himself from it. That's important because we say of course that he did everything formally as well and I'm going to come to that in a minute. But it's important that he expressed the moral outrage and conveyed to a person who was his subordinate within the inspection team, that's Namik Dzankovic, conveyed to him in clear terms how -- that he disapproved of this. Because, of course, it is possible in theory for someone to issue a mere order of some sort, I mean a routine order that conveys nothing much other than its routineness. That wasn't the case here. Here Halilovic put a moral emphasis on what he was asking his security officer from the inspection team to do, and that's Dzankovic. Your Honours, it's also apparent that apart from speaking to Dzankovic as he did and dealing with him and activating the involvement of Dzankovic and his organisation, the SVB, Halilovic also reported to Delic. He says he did in his book, D281. No precise time is put on that, but it's uncontested that he contacted Delic. The Prosecution, had they wanted to contest that, had to call Commander Delic. Now, again it's their choice and they don't have to. There's no cheating connected to that. It's at prosecutorial discretion. But that's the choice they made and as a result you've got undisputed comment by Halilovic to the effect that he advised Delic. After that time we say Halilovic conducted himself appropriately. There is no evidence at all I apart from the outrageous claim of Ramiz Delalic that Halilovic covered up the crime or did anything positively evil in respect to it. And as to Ramiz Delalic, for reasons we've already said, you just reject his evidence. He's a stain, frankly, on this case, Ramiz Delalic. He got inside the investigation. He helped Nikolai Mikhailov collecting the witnesses and what we say is he's not to be believed. Now, the failure to punish. I'm coming to the details of that. The duration pleaded by the Prosecution for a duty on Halilovic at that time ends on 19th September, pursuant to the indictment so that Halilovic's time to act seems to be between his actual notice on the night of the 9th and the time when he ceases to be in charge, if you make that finding. Of course if you don't make that finding it's all finished, on 19th of September. Now, the Defence says that our -- our defence to all this is a very simple one, a very straightforward one, a very easy one to comprehend. It is that Halilovic called in the SVB to investigate this crime. The SVB is an acronym for the military security service. I'll call it the SVB. We've all been calling it that throughout. Now, the brief facts are that Halilovic told Dzankovic that he wanted him to find out information about it and communicate to him in Sarajevo about it. The context in which Mr. Halilovic did that was that it was the fact that Dzankovic had already commenced to do some work. He'd already sent a report to Sarajevo, a short one, not the big one that's in evidence, but a short one to Sarajevo. And so that the investigation was already underway. Now, it's important to note this: The Prosecution made a complaint that the order by Halilovic was an oral order and was vague in nature. Well, it had to be an oral order because it had to be immediate. He had to tell him straight away. That's what he did. Can you imagine the reaction of the Prosecutors if he had a delay to write an order? That would have been held against him and he would have had an obligation to do an oral order. It reflects what we say is a pattern of opportunistic argument-- again, the prosecutors have got a job to do, and we are criticising the implications of guilt for Halilovic, it's not an attack on the Prosecutors personally in the least -- but we say it means that their argument ought to be regarded as weaker. Your Honours, apart from it being -- the criticism of it being an oral order and a vague order, the fact is there's no format set out by which such communication should happen, nowhere. The Prosecutor didn't point you to or use any form of words that should have been used. To suggest that it's vague is a criticism by the Prosecutor in the atmosphere. It's rather like calling Witness J incoherent. It's just a criticism, but it's not founded in evidence anywhere. But to proceed with this part of the indictment. When Dzankovic spoke to Halilovic, the matter had already been reported to Sarajevo by Dzankovic and therefore, pursuant to the chain of command, that had to have been communicated to Rasim Delic. It had to be. Look at Exhibit D143. The SVB, the military security service, reports up its own professional chain, and we've already heard evidence about that. But when it gets to Jusuf Jasarevic, the head, that organ reports to the commander. So, Your Honours, what we say is that Halilovic did what was necessary in the circumstances. And thus I'll turn to the rules, the SVB rules. Now, let me just explain why it is the Defence places such store on these rules. Firstly, of course, you are not here to adjudicate on local Bosnian law. Secondly, although all of us in the court have now achieved a working knowledge of these rules we are not seeking to give some expert position about what one provision might mean. Why it matters is this: These rules provide the SVB, the military security service, with the full competence to do what was necessary to investigate murder. If you want as a military commander to catch a murderer, you turn to the experts who have got the full power to look into it and do everything that is required. The SVB can activate the military police. They've got a direct power under Section 7 to deal with military police and direct their work in professional matters. The Prosecutors also -- sorry, the -- pardon me. The SVB also has the power to call in an investigating judge or a military prosecutor. And I just ask you to jump forward for one second to when Dzankovic wrote his proposals on the 13th. It's exactly what he did in the second point of those proposals that he wrote out. He said, Send a mixed team from Sarajevo including an investigative judge. The SVB had that power. In other words, and I raise that because I don't want it to be said and I don't want to counter any suggestion by the Prosecutors. It may be overreaction by the Defence because they don't seem to have raised this anymore, but I want to shut that gate. It shouldn't be said that Halilovic had some free-standing obligation to go off and get military prosecutors or other organs. The fact is the SVB had all that power and they were the experts and knew when and how it should be done. And although it may be said that Halilovic-- he may not have been a lawyer, he may not have known every detail of all this, he must have expected that the SVB would be competent and able to do their job. I just want to point out one thing from the Rules, and this is the only point of the rules I'll go to. At paragraph 40, it provides the basis upon which the SVB involves itself -- on what basis the SVB involves itself in an investigation. At para 40, it says: "When there is reasonable suspicion that a criminal offence, triable by military courts"-- I'm at paragraph 40, I'm sorry, Your Honours -- "has been committed, officers of the military security service must take the necessary measure to find the perpetrator." That tells you that the obligation of the SVB is a free-standing one. They've got that obligation whether or not the commander tells them. They have that obligation. That doesn't absolve a commander of the obligation to tell them, that's quite a different question. It's not disputed by the Defence either; a commander does have the obligation to do what's necessary to make sure that they're on notice. That obligation doesn't arise from the SVB rules but it seems to have been a practice. It's not sourced in a rule but Karavelic says it's there and everyone seems to have acted in accordance with it. But what's important is there's no form of words that has to be used. It's really a question of putting the SVB -- what a commander has got to do is put the SVB in a reasonable position, where it's got reasonable suspicion, where it's empowered to act. And on no view of things could Halilovic have done any less than that. What he did was enough to activate the SVB. What he told Dzankovic was, plainly, enough. It was plainly aimed at doing that, and it plainly did do that. Therefore Halilovic started the ball rolling in his own mind. He did everything he had to do. He told the SVB to investigate and that's what they did. Now, Your Honours, these rules should have been in evidence from the beginning and we do make a criticism of the Prosecution here because they put in evidence instead the military discipline rules that have got absolutely nothing to do with this. You don't investigate these crimes by using the military discipline powers. Those are powers that apt to preserve discipline within a unit involving tiny remedies and discretionary application of those rules. And we've got a section there, but I'm not going to say anything more about it. We do make the point that this was obviously something that was central and while it wasn't a part of the Prosecution case -- well, we don't know why it wasn't but obviously it should have been because this was the crunch. If there's supposed to be a failure to punish, this issue had to be dealt with, and the Prosecution case just simply sidestepped and referred to a body of rules that had nothing to do with the case at all and had the function of obscuring the jobs that Your Honours have to do. Very well, that is all you need to hear from me on the topic of the extent of those rules there. But I do draw your attention to Exhibit D464 which is the agreed facts between the parties concerning the effect of these rules and also to the Defence brief --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I've been asked to slow down. The Defence brief, 624 to 626 inclusive. The Prosecution -- sorry, the SVB had the power to take necessary measures. And that's enough. That's the -- that's the powers they need. Take necessary measures. And that's what they did. My learned friend Mr. Mettraux, when he comes to the legal part that will be with us in about 30 minutes, perhaps a little over that, is going to take you to some quotes concerning that and how a commander should deal with it in a general sense. But I ask you to regard the SVB rules not as some sort of legal trick behind which commanders shelter but as an enabling piece of legislation, as something that permits the investigation. It must be remembered the chaos that beset the Bosnian army. Imposing these rules, bringing these rules in -- and the evidence is that Halilovic had a major role in introducing these rules. Bringing these rules in was a positive step forward for disciplining the army and for human rights generally. It allowed commanders to do what they're supposed to do. Without that you would have a situation that commanders had international obligations of various sorts with no ability whatsoever to carry them out, none. And this system had to be supported. There's a positive rule of law needed for commanders to go through the channels. You can't have Ramiz Delalic putting a gun to his soldiers' head and saying confess or I'll shoot you. Line up -- that's if he really did that. There's a question whether that was a bona fide line-up. But that sort of justice isn't just -- you've got to go through the right channels. And the Prosecution can't urge that an accused man has failed to do what he should do just because he stuck to the official channels. He should stick to the official channels. So Halilovic was entitled -- the effect of all that was the SVB would investigate the crime. Halilovic was entitled to trust them. The SVB didn't consist of Namik Dzankovic alone. The Prosecution made an attack on Namik Dzankovic. The Defence is not here to defend Dzankovic but we want to make this comment: He was okay. He did his best. He did what he could. There was a bit of criticism, post facto criticism by Jusuf Jasarevic. There could be all sorts of reasons for that, but in the end Jasarevic did not say that he was a person lacking integrity and he said that he tried his best. What's most important about that, however, is that never was Dzankovic said at the time to be incompetent. Halilovic was entitled to count on Dzankovic. He was -- Dzankovic was joined to the team by order of Rasim Delic on the specific recommendation of Jusuf Jasarevic, the head of the service. There is no basis on which Halilovic could have concluded that there was something wrong with Dzankovic, that Dzankovic was going to do a bad job, that Dzankovic was somehow hopeless. They didn't prove that. They made criticisms of what Dzankovic did but they didn't actually point to anything specifically wrong that Halilovic knew about. The next issue that's important is that Halilovic made it quite plain that Dzankovic's investigation ought to be in cooperation with the civilian authorities. In the Defence final brief at paragraph 638 we extracted a part of a conversation between Halilovic and Dzankovic when Dzankovic explained some of the things he had already done and Dzankovic's's help that he gave and Halilovic said: "Great. Then you can continue to work together." Specific instructions. That common sharing of the tasks is a theme. Now, later on you might think that some of the police who gave evidence were perhaps-- I'm inclined to say that they didn't play much of a part, didn't have orders to do so. But the record at the time speaks for itself and the evidence of Dzankovic is also very decisive on this topic: That they worked together. And Halilovic was heavily committed wherever he was. But what Jasarevic does in D221 and D235 is he gives tasks to the security service of the 1st Corps and he explained that in evidence. In our brief we've set this out, as we just don't have time, it's a wonderful thing to read out, but it's long and I'm not going to. But in the brief we've revealed a passage in cross-examination from him which is important. Your Honours, the Prosecution were in the position therefore, once that evidence was in, that it's obvious that the investigation grew beyond giving it to Dzankovic and transferred over to the 1st Corps. If the Prosecution seriously wanted to contest that proposition which arises not by implication but by the direct evidence of Jasarevic, direct evidence, if they wanted to contest that, they shouldn't have withdrawn the chief of security of the 1st Corps, Sacir Arnautovic. If they seriously wanted to contest that inference, why are they taking away the only person who can say? The answer to that question is this: There's unopposed evidence that the 1st Corps did pursue the investigation. We don't know to what extent because they withdrew the witness. But Sacir Arnautovic existed because he's the signature on some of that operative information that you've got. And again we note this: The Prosecutor can withdraw who they wish. They've not prosecutorial discretion, but let them say you that they are somehow ministers of justice. They're an adversarial party here, and they're giving you the picture they want you to have, which they're entitled to do in an adversarial system. But when they invite you to draw an inference, you have to consider whether you're being given the full picture or whether you are being given an adversarial picture. You have to consider that, and here is an example of exactly why you would not draw the inference they ask you. In any event, we say the inference is crushing. Very well. It's also the fact that Jasarevic says on the 3rd -- 2nd of March at page 34, he says that the Operation Trebevic was speeded up by the events in Grabovica. Turning to Dzankovic, he did the best he could. Your Honours, we're definitely going to hurry up now. Dzankovic did well. He sent reports on the 9th, he reported to Karic, he received instructions from Karic. Your Honours, he went to Grabovica twice. Prosecution relied on him being shut out of Grabovica once, and it's true you've got to consider what that means. The answer is this: He didn't have his identification card, nor did he have a uniform. He had a pilot uniform and no identification card. And any sinister connotation of him being stopped at that checkpoint is dispelled because shortly after that he did go to the village and he did get into the village and he did try to speak to witnesses, one named one Samir Peco, and Mr. Solakovic, the commander. And we don't know what the role of Solakovic in all of this was, but we do know he was worried about civilians and trying to protect them, so he's a person of good will but he would not talk. So Dzankovic liaised with police, and we do not agree and we submit that you shouldn't agree with the Prosecution's case that the investigation was segmented Salihamidzic actually went to the village with a military policeman, Sead Kurt, and we've been through those matters and they're in the brief. Your Honours, I won't go to D215 in detail. You have that. It's behind tab 15. But I ask you to look at the proposals made by Dzankovic. They were sensible proposals. That's part of his job. Make a plan, decide how we're going to deal with this matter. Read those proposals. Now, Jusuf Jasarevic said they weren't practical in reality, but Dzankovic then waited to see what would come with that. Jasarevic tells us what he didn't get that letter dated the 13th until the 20th. Halilovic is out of the picture by then. If Dzankovic showed some inaction, the Prosecutors want to say that he did show some inaction in that time, if he did, he was waiting until his boss told him what to do. He sent that report. It's D215. He was entitled to wait. The Prosecution were critical because they said that necessary and reasonable measures were not taken. In the indictment they specified at paragraphs 15 and 34 that there should have been immediate arrest of the suspects ordered by Halilovic and an investigation ordered. Well, the Defence responds to that by saying, number one, they did. Halilovic did order an investigation and that disposes of that easily. As to the question of ordering the immediate arrest of the suspects, there are a number of big problems with that. We can go all day on that topic, and I'll try to keep it as limited as I can. Number one, there weren't any suspects. Mr. Re yesterday -- I'm sorry. Yesterday, Your Honour, it was suggested that it would have been easy to find out. But you don't just get the local plumber to go and fix the local problem in Grabovica. Down there was Ramiz Delalic and his men. He behaved in a threatening way. Zuka's soldier had a throat cut, and it wasn't that easy to find things out. Witness D didn't admit that he was right there when the shooting of Pero Maric happened until he was interviewed by Ms. Chana here at the Tribunal, having made many statements before, lying ones. He said he had an order from the Court not to tell anyone. But when the Prosecutor says it's easy to find out, that's just a comment in thin atmosphere, it's not the truth. In the pre-trial brief other duties were alleged. We say it was not sensible, necessary, or reasonable to enter the village by force. Now, a number of complaints can be covered by that. We say, first of all, it's not proved that the police had the resources. Two platoons of local military police do not add up to sufficient force to take on Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and his heavily armed troop of Sarajevo soldiers. The Prosecution did not seek to lead that it was possible. And, Your Honours, there is a number of real difficulties with taking a forcible action. And I'll list them now, since the Prosecution here would wish to say that they had an interest in the well-being of civilians. There was civilians living on the other side of that river, and a battle in Grabovica on the right bank does not confine to the right bank when the bullets are flying. There was a genuine danger if anyone tried to have a fight in Grabovica that the civilians living on the other side would be in danger, nor is it possible to say they could go anywhere else. The whole point was: There wasn't anywhere to go, everywhere was full. If you tried to force your way into the village, you endangered civilians, you endangered the troops, you endangered the operation, you endangered the morale of the army, you caused the danger of escalation, you endangered the relief of Mostar. We ask Your Honours to look at D276 which is behind tab 17. Have a look at that. That's the danger that was facing the troops, anyone who wanted to go into the village. There was a danger of revolt, there was a danger of bloodshed. And it would not have helped to go into the village because it hasn't been proved that there were people there who were prepared to make statements. Indeed, when Dzankovic got in, even men of the 2nd Independent Battalion didn't want to make statements. If there was a battle it would wreck the crime scene. In any event, the idea - and we've made this point in the brief - the idea of crime scene experts inspecting busily away with their equipment while Ramiz Delalic, Malco, and others fought with the local Jablanica military police, assuming they were prepared to help, is just a ludicrous idea. It can't be right. There's got to be some level of reality. And perhaps I'll put it another way. That's a submission from me, it's my comment, and it's not much use to you. There's got to be evidence that that was possible before you could say that that was a failure. It's got to be given some reality. And what we'd say in legal terms is it wasn't necessary or reasonable, that alleged measure. The status report is another thing that Halilovic is supposed to have called for. That's a new concept, the status report, it's not in international humanitarian law. It's not in Bosnian law. It's a Prosecution invention. The SVB had full power to investigate, they didn't need to report back to their commander, and Karavelic made it clear, again as we've stressed in our brief, that it wasn't necessary or usual to do that. You could easily have a situation where a crime occurred in a unit and the commander might be implicated in it. The SVB doesn't have to report back to the commander and can't be required to in all circumstances. As we said, D231 makes it clear that there was an investigation going on at that time. Your Honours, by the time Halilovic finished his work, whatever that work was, in Herzegovina on the 19th or 20th of September, this investigation had passed way out of local control and existed contemporaneously with Dzankovic in Herzegovina, with the 1st Corps in Sarajevo, and with other units. What happened to it after that is not relevant, although we might be inclined to criticise Mr. Zebic's characterisation of certain orders and say that Dzankovic did right and did everything he could, we just refer you to our brief to deal with the matters that come afterwards. Therefore, we say that Halilovic did everything that was reasonably open to him. We say that the Prosecution have identified artificial requirements which do not have a proper source in law anywhere, which were not pleaded, and which upon proper analysis are neither necessary nor reasonable, and ignore the prevailing realities that Ramiz Delalic was deliberately blocking this investigation with the threat of violence and revolt. And if you look at D226, you will see how local -- how the military security service regarded that situation at the time. No one at the time thought that the village should be crashed. I turn, finally, to the crime at Uzdol and the allegations of the Prosecutor that there was a failure to investigate this crime. Could I just comment this, Your Honour, I'm not dealing with the crime scene. We've said what we had to say about it in the brief. It's just too short of time, and we rely on what we say in the brief. Concerning with -- concerning Uzdol, as a preliminary matter, Your Honours will have to consider those issues, whether there was a crime by soldiers as opposed to by police. You might impose a mens rea test. It's very difficult to deal with so many victims and hard to know what's a good working test. You might decide when you look at those victims you can rule them out if you can't be sure of the mens rea of the killing -- the shooter, because at Uzdol they are all shot except for two, and it's not the Defence case that they were killed by bombs. In any event, I won't go into the crime scene now. Your Honours, we say that there's -- in relation to Uzdol we say that there was a lack of effective control, that Halilovic didn't have effective control. We also say there's a grave doubt over the notice of Halilovic, both in terms of the quality of the notice of Halilovic and the timing of the notice of Halilovic. And finally, we say there was no failure to take any reasonable or necessary measure. What we say is there was an investigation at all levels. We say that no realistic step has been identified which Halilovic had the duty to take and failed to take. And now we go into the details of that. The notice of Halilovic is flawed. The Prosecution case is imprecise. They rely -- it's not their fault. The evidence is imprecise, and I don't mean that as a criticism on the Prosecutor. Their allegation is, based on Halilovic's own book, that he found out several days later. That can't be placed in any precise framework. It may be in the time frame between the 18th and 20th of September. But you couldn't find, based on what Halilovic says, that it was before that time. Now, we say the timing of this could well be fatal to the Prosecution case on its own. It's a matter you'll have to consider. It's a short point but it's an important one. If you make a finding that Halilovic's effective control of those troops ended on the 15th or 16th of September, then you're not in a position to say that he had any power over those troops whatsoever at the time he found out, even if you found he was in effective control at the time of the battle. The notice that Halilovic actually had is of uncertain quality. He himself described it as illegal acts, but that's a description in 1995 after there's more truth known about it then there was at the time. There's no basis to doubt his bona fides that he wanted Buza to be dealt with in relation to this matter. But the allegations themselves were doubtful and they came from doubtful sources. Radio Rama is not a trustworthy source. If you hear your news from radio Rama, you are not on notice that it actually happened or that there's a strong likelihood that it happened. It's just a rumour if it comes from Radio Rama, probably given the viewpoint that those on the Bosnian side would take, probably false, simply because it came from that source. The BBC may well have broadcast, as they say, the evidence is that Kate Adie broadcast in the English language, and the evidence here is that Halilovic doesn't speak it. There's no evidence that Halilovic condoned or acquiesced in these crimes it in the least. So that if you find he was in effective control and that he didn't take enough steps, you wouldn't find that he condoned or acquiesced, that he had that, if you like, acquiescing state of mind that goes along with conviction here. But, Your Honours, as was apparent with our case, there was an investigation into this crime. And the fact that it didn't reveal everything that the Prosecution now allege is not a bar to it being a full and proper investigation. It began before Halilovic found about these crimes. Never did anyone at the time call upon Halilovic to participate,. The president, Commander Delic, Salko Gusic, the 6th Corps commander, who later on realised that Halilovic must have been in command of the Prozor Independent Battalion. None of them thought that Halilovic should play a part. None of them directed correspondence to him or asked him to do anything or to play any part or to give any information. Your Honours, by virtue of the material behind tab 12 and 18 on the 16th of September, Stjepan Siber, deputy for Delic, made an inquiry of the 6th Corps. On the same day by Exhibit 227 Jusuf Jasarevic made an inquiry to his SVB operative, Nermin Eminovic, a much troubled witness who had a great deal on his plate at the time. And whilst the Defence did dispute some of his evidence you had to have some sympathy with Mr. Eminovic and the position he was in as commander of the 6th Corps Security Service at that time. Gusic did not say when he received that correspondence, Don't send it to me, send it to Halilovic. He didn't refer it to Halilovic or mention it to Halilovic. Your Honours, the response at the top level of the Bosnian army was prompt, efficient, and bona fide. They called for reports. They acted on the reports. At the highest level, no more can be done. Some of those reports are in evidence, D232, D236. They are behind tabs 20 and 21. It's quite clear that at the top levels of the Bosnian army, everyone reacted properly. And Halilovic, whatever view you take of him as a commander, is at the top level. He is not down at the battalion command level. And therefore, if Halilovic was involved, he would have done and could have done only those high-level steps, calling for reports and so on. Now they were called for. So there is no step that could have been taken that was failed to be taken at that high level, and there's no basis for doubting the bona fides of what was said. Your Honours, if it be concluded that the material from Radio Rama put them on notice that they should call for an inquiry, well, the answer to that is that at the high levels the Bosnian army did react appropriately. Witness J was able to explain in relation to two of those reports, D232 and D236, where he thought they got their information from and which parts of his information had been put into that report. Obviously they weren't his reports, and he didn't write them and he didn't agree with everything that's in them. The SVB, Your Honours, again did its job. Eminovic had to make inquiries and that's what he did. Down at the Prozor Independent Battalion there was also an inquiry. Witness J gave evidence about this; he was a good witness. It's a rhetorical question and contains its own answer. Why didn't, the investigator, Mikhailov find this man? We don't know because he wasn't called. But he was obviously a central person. The Prosecution tactics in this particular Prosecution, this particular part of the case called for criticism because what they did was to withdraw almost every witness who knew anything about it, call two members of the Bosnian army, both with pseudonyms, witnesses G and H, and elicit from them that they didn't know -- well, elicit from one that they don't know about an investigation and from that ask you, so it would appear, to infer that there wasn't an investigation. They didn't run at that time, Your Honours, or plead or suggest this cover-up theory. That cover-up theory is new. Witness J came and gave evidence; it was good evidence. We say that in awful circumstances bona fide he took 15 statements, he spoke to a number of soldiers. It could have been about 100 but he said that wasn't clear. He reported to the SVB. He helped Buza to compile a report, D149, it's in evidence, four to five reports were produced by him and his colleagues -- him and/or his colleagues. He spoke to the president. He had good reasons to believe the soldiers' stories. He thought there was house-to-house fighting and there was. He had heard the HVO soldiers on the radio criticising each other for shelling civilians. The fact that the civilians on display in this case were not killed by shells does not remove the reality of Mr. -- Witness J's perception of shelling. And there was visible devastation and smoke. Now, we say the Prosecution did not prove the absence of shelling. You can look to Defence Exhibit D318 which is Croatian -- sorry, HVO battle reports which refer to shelling being done by themselves. And we haven't got time. I invite you to look at those reports. There was an attack on Witness J as part of the cover-up but we say -- and I don't mean this as a personal attack, the Prosecutors have got to do their job, but it was a desperate situation for the Prosecutors. They had no real basis for that attack. There was no basis for saying he was part of the cover-up. They shouldn't have made that attack without a basis, and we say they don't have it. The incoherence allegation was particularly unfair, and we invite you to look at his evidence and decide whether it's the questions or the answers that are unfair -- that are incoherent, but he, we submit, was a crystal clear witness upon whom you can rely. He was no whitewasher. He did come to the view that some soldiers had something on their conscience, and he told you that. There was nothing more he could have done. The Prosecution flirted, and I use that term advisedly, they flirted with the idea that perhaps contacts could have been made with the HVO, that other material could have been gained. Well, to suggest that the HVO would have assisted is not borne out by the evidence. That's why Witness K was called. He came from a humanitarian organisation, and he was given a manipulated and partial picture when he got to the village where he was given a witness who he formed the view -- and he was a very sympathetic witness to the people he was going to see. He wanted to help. But he was given false information by an alleged eyewitness that he formed the view was just a put-up job. He was not given cooperation, not allowed to speak to the eyewitnesses and survivors. Why was that? Because there was a battle in the village and because that wasn't in the interests of those authorities at the time to reveal that there was such a battle. And saying that does not diminish the fact, if you find there were murders, that there were murders. The reality or otherwise of killings in -- in Uzdol is not at issue here. What's at issue in this part of the submission is whether or not Witness J was entitled to come to the views that he did and whether it looks like a cover-up. And the fact is it just doesn't look like a cover-up. The Prosecution did not identify steps that were failed to be taken. They didn't plead such steps, they didn't identify them at any time. And again, there is just this atmosphere that they'll think them up as intelligent lawyers at a later time rather than saying that there's a sensible source for these obligations, and where do humans in horrible situations turn to find out their obligations find these allegations? They don't have the benefit of the learned Prosecutors to help them at that time. They just have to do the best they can, and their investigators. Your Honours, I would now seek to hand the microphone to Mr. Mettraux in relation to some legal matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Within the next half-hour, the Defence would like to make a number of legal submissions and we don't intend to re-tell this Trial Chamber our submissions as they appear in the final brief, but simply to emphasise on the line a number of matters which are of particular interest we believe. The first such matter is an issue already touched upon by lead counsel for the Defence, which concerned the relationship which must be shown to exist between the accused on the one hand and the alleged perpetrator on the other. We do not believe that the issue of effective control needs any specification from the legal point of view. As for effective control, Your Honour, it's been defined on many occasions as "the material ability to prevent and punish crimes." It is a relationship of authority which goes unquestioned between two poles, one that gives order and the other that obeys. In such a relationship, in effect, one of the power loses the ability to disagree with the other. What the Defence submits and what the law supports is that short of giving a criminal order, which the subordinate would be bound under the laws of war to rebel and refuse to implement, effective control implies an enforceable expectation of obedience on the parts of the subordinates, and a mere expectation of compliance on the part of the superior. Effective control may also be characterised perhaps in a different way as the ability of an individual to exercise unquestioned authority over the otherwise free will of another person and to enforce that authority, if need be. The Appeals Chamber has made it clear in the Tribunal that the sort of or the degree of authority which the commander must be able to exercise over that subordinate is one equivalent to a de jure sort of authority which -- one which you would find in a normal functioning army. Effective control is not the same as an ability to convince, to prompt, or to influence, nor is it the equivalent of an availability of a sanction on the commander, however remote. Lead counsel has also pointed out that the crucial and critical difference between a power to influence, even though the Appeals Chamber has substantial influence, would not suffice to amount to effective control. What must be shown is, as was just pointed out before, that one party has lost the ability to disagree with the other party, with the orders, to question the order, or to choose to disobey the order. But rather than to give you some abstract definition of what effective control means under international humanitarian law, we would like to point to three very clear examples of judgements in this Tribunal where Trial Chambers had to decide that very matter: Where does the line between influence and effective control lie? And what we suggest is those three decisions, the Celebici Trial Chamber judgement, the Kvocka Trial Chamber and the Kordic judgements, make it clear where the line lies, and those three judgements should give you a snapshot of the law as it should apply to this case. In the Kvocka case the Trial Chamber held that Mr. Kvocka did not have effective control despite the following. He was found to have had clear and broad authority and influence within the camp. Former inmates testify and an inmate who had known him before the war, he assumed Mr. Kvocka had been the commander of the camp. A number of guards made it clear that they could not allow certain things to happen within the camp without the approval of Mr. Kvocka. Mr. Kvocka himself addressed prisoners and told them he was in charge; he replaced the camp commander in his absence and he passed on his orders. He was also seen and heard giving orders to camp guards, and despite all of the above he was found not to be in effective control of the alleged perpetrator. That finding was upheld on appeal. The same approach was adopted by the Celebici Trial Chamber earlier where the Trial Chamber made the finding that Mr. Delalic had exercised much authority and was greatly respected within his community. There was evidence that he was the objective, general recognition and appreciation, paragraph 651 of the trial judgement, that he had been granted some special authorisation, for example to negotiate and conclude contracts on behalf of the presidency, that he was a well-placed individual, an influential one, paragraph 658. He was also appointed as coordinator of the Konjic municipality defence forces, which empowered him in turn to directly coordinate the work of defence forces in Konjic. Mr. Delalic signed various orders. He participated in military operations and ceremonies and was the commander of a tactical group. There again, the Trial Chamber finds that this influence, this substantial influence, was not enough to amount to effective control. The Kordic trial judgement is perhaps even more revealing for Your Honours and perhaps a better source than the previous two -- for the present purposes. Mr. Kordic was said to be a politician with tremendous influence and power. It was found by the Trial Chamber that he had an important position in the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, that he played an important role in military matters, even at time issuing orders and exercising authority over HVO forces. He was found to have had substantial influence over those who are said to have committed the crimes. The Trial Chamber found that he was not in effective control of the troop and, again, the Trial Chamber [sic] upheld that finding. That, Your Honour, is what we suggest is the matrix within which you will have to assess the evidence in this case and also the matrix, we suggest, that should allow you to resist any attempt made to dilute the meaning and significance of effective control. Effective control is also a relationship between persons, between the accused on the one hand and the alleged perpetrators on the other; it is not a relationship between the accused and a unit or a military entity. What the Prosecution must establish is a personal relationship, be it an indirect one, be it one that goes through several levels of military hierarchy or other sort of hierarchy. But it is not a relationship of a man over a brigade or unit. Lead counsel has also noted, and I will not spend a great amount of time on this issue, effective control must be established, the Appeals Chamber has made clear, at the time when the crimes were being committed, not before, not after. What that means in practice - evidentially is very important - is this case: The Trial Chamber will have to make a finding that as of the 8th or 9th of September, 1993, as far as the 9th Brigade is concerned, and the 14th as far as the Prozor Independent Battalion is concerned, Mr. Halilovic had asserted his effective control over those troops. And in that regard I will come back on this issue. The evidence relied upon by the Prosecution to establish effective control is quite revealing. At paragraph 181 of their final brief the Prosecution mentions no less than seven orders attributed to Mr. Halilovic and which the Prosecution says are relevant to establishing effective control. Six of those orders, Your Honour, have been issued after the incidents. They are, therefore, evidentially irrelevant. As for the seventh order, it's been addressed by Mr. Morrissey, it is P161, the order of the 2nd of September, and I will not come back on this issue. Another point which was already made by my lead counsel, and I simply reiterate it, the other side of the coin of that requirement is that the obligation of a commander to act only lasts for as long as he is under the effective control -- as he is in effective control of the alleged perpetrators. Concerning, more specifically, the manner in which the Prosecution proposes to establish effective control, they list, as I have just mentioned, a number of orders, as allegedly being relevant to that determination. I have already pointed out the problem of the time of those orders. But you will have to look at each and every order and consider their content to consider whether they are indeed evidentially relevant to the finding of effective control. And what the Prosecution would have to establish is, firstly, that it's an order which has been given or signed by the accused; it was an order signed to the relevant people. When you do that assessment you also have to look at the capacity in which Mr. Halilovic, in this case, signed those orders. That was the position of the Celebici Trial Chamber, and a very sound one. And a point that we want to make here concerned orders which are being signed by Chief of Staff. And the high command court, the post-Nuremberg, based in Nuremberg court, said this and was quoted by saying this also by the Celebici Trial Chamber about orders being signed by Chief of Staff. "The Chief of Staff does not have command authority in the chain of command. An order of his own signature does not have authority for subordinates in the chain of command." The orders, I have already pointed out, must be given directly or indirectly to the alleged perpetrators, not to third parties. They must be binding orders, not recommendation or instruction. Those are not revealing of any exercise of authority or power over those troops. Those orders must also be shown by evidence to have been complied with, obeyed. Yesterday the Prosecution suggested this: The mere fact that an order is not obeyed is not indicative of a lack of effective control. Clearly that is wrong. And the Appeals Chamber said so in the Blaskic appeals judgement, where it says: "Proof is required that the accused was not only able to issue orders but that the orders were actually followed." It's paragraph 69, and that's a position which was shared in another judgement, the Kordic Trial Chamber, for instance. Lead Counsel has also pointed out that the order must reveal the exercise of the accused's own power, not that he's exercising anyone else's power. There again, I direct Your Honour to the Celebici trial judgement where the orders which were signed or passed on by Mr. Delalic were seen as merely "state of intermediate implementation." Finally "those orders must be indicative" bears some indicia of an exercise of power, of authority. They may not simply be routine orders.
