I'll quickly move on, for lack of time, to the second issue, Your Honour, that of mens rea. The lead counsel for the Defence has already pointed out to the test as far as failure to prevent is concerned. This is that of the substantial likelihood. This is a test which has been applied in other circumstances and in particular in the Strugar Trial Chamber judgement. What the Prosecution will point out to you and what they have done in their brief is that they have appealed this finding of the Trial Chamber. What we say is this is a correct statement of the law as it existed at the time. This finding is correct and not only is it correct, it's supported by the finding of the Appeals Chamber at paragraph 41 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber, which says, "not as the Prosecution would have it but this is a requirement that applies only to ordering, pursuant to 7(1), but to all form of liability for serious violations of international law." This is what the Blaskic Appeals Chamber said, this is what the Strugar Trial Chamber has repeated. Concerning the nature of the knowledge which Mr. Halilovic in this case must be shown to have had is that of the substantial likelihood of murders, not of any illegal conduct, not of some illegal act or some criminal tendencies or criminal propensity. He must be shown to have had knowledge or sufficient notice of the substantial likelihood of murder. And I direct Your Honour to the very clear and very detailed finding of the Appeals Chamber in Krnojelac, in relation to findings that were made by the Trial Chamber in relation to torture, where the Appeals Chamber said, in essence, that the finding that Mr. Krnojelac could be convicted as a commander for torture based on knowledge that he had of beating committed by his subordinates without more was not sufficient. He had to know of this special purpose which is required by the crime of torture. This is an element. In this case, the Prosecution will have to show that Mr. Halilovic at the relevant time knew of all of the elements of the definition of murder, including the specific state of mind required for that offence. They've failed. Concerning the timing of knowledge, my lead counsel has already pointed out, and I will not stop here, knowledge must be established at the time prior to the alleged failure. In fact, it is knowledge or notice, as defined by the Appeals Chamber, which triggers his obligation to act. I will stop, however, for a second to emphasise a point a bit more as far as failure to prevent is concerned. The Statute is quite clear about the moment or the immediacy that must exist between the acquisition of knowledge on the one hand and the crime that is about to happen. This is those word -- those words are, "are about to happen." What the Prosecution is apparently attempting to do now is to make a requirement of general knowledge of something that exists out there and which would have given at some stage, and specified as we've noted, of specific knowledge. Well, the Rule doesn't require prophetic powers on the parts of the accused. It doesn't do that. The Kordic/Krnojelac Trial Chamber has made it very clear what "are about to be committed" means, and I will simply quote from the judgement, paragraph 445: "The duty to prevent should be understood as resting on a superior at any stage before the commission of a subordinate crime if he acquires knowledge that such a crime is being prepared or planned or when he has reasonable ground to suspect subordinate crimes." This is when the obligation is triggered, when he knows that steps are being taken, that crimes are on the verge of being committed. That finding of the Kordic Trial Chamber was repeated in the, for instance, the Hadzihasanovic Rule 98 bis decision, a recent one, at paragraph 166. A remote or uncertain possibility that a crime might at some stage, undefined, unspecified, be committed is not enough under Article 7(3). This is not what the law provides for. Lead counsel has also highlighted the danger of hindsight in those matters, and indeed there is a serious danger that everyone would naturally perhaps be tempted to look at what happened and bring it back to the relevant time. Well, that temptation should be resisted, and I refer Your Honour to a US State Department -- or Department of Defence report to Congress on the conduct in the Persian Gulf War, which we cited in our brief and which says this: "Leaders and commanders necessarily have to make decisions on the basis of their assessment of the information reasonably available to them at the time rather than what is determined in hindsight." In addition to the knowledge already mentioned, the accused must be shown to have intended not to act, as he was required to do, with or despite that knowledge. In the language of the Hostage court, another post-Nuremberg case, "there must be proof of a positive covert act or omission from which a guilty intent can be inferred. There can be no crime large or small without an evil mind." In other words, punishment is the consequence of wickedness. "Neither in philosophical speculation nor in relation to religion or moral sentiment would any people in any age allow that a man should be deemed guilty unless his mind is so." In our brief, Your Honour, we have also pointed out that the failure of the accused must be intentional in the sense of being both voluntary and deliberate. Yesterday, however, in its closing argument the Prosecution has suggested that the Defence had pointed out to no authority for its, essentially, allegation. And the Prosecution pointed Your Honour to paragraph 616 of our final brief. And the Prosecution is quite correct, there was no authority in this paragraph. The authority for the element of acquiescences is to be found in 426 to 428 of our brief, and I will briefly summarise it here: "In the high command case in relation to the accused Von Leeb, the court said that he must be shown both to have had knowledge and to have been connected with certain criminal acts, either by way of participation or criminal acquiescences." The hostage case in the case of Foertsch, another accused talks about consenting part in the crime, whereas, for -- in the judgement where it says "approve of the action of his subordinates." The Flick case, "knowledge and approval." The Toyoda case, "permitted atrocities." And closer to us, in the Tribunal, the Strugar trial judgement, paragraph 439, "the accused was, at the very least by acquiescence a participant in the arrangement by which Admiral Jokic undertook his sham investigation and sham disciplinary action." At the ICTR Musema trial judgement, paragraph 131, where the Trial Chamber mentioned "tantamount to acquiescence or even malicious intent." This is the authority the Defence is relying on. I'm sure that the Trial Chamber would be able to find some others, but the Prosecution is pointing to none to the contrary. This is a requirement of customary international law. Furthermore and one quick point in passing, knowledge may not be presumed and superior responsibility does not arise from failure to act in spite of knowledge. Knowledge must be established beyond reasonable doubt. If it is inferred it must be the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the evidence. And the facts upon which that inference is being drawn must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. An inference of knowledge may not be made based on the position only, and I refer Your Honour to the finding of the IMT in Nuremberg, the military tribunal: "In relation to the absent although judged Mr. Borman, the evidence does not show that Borman knew of Hitler's plan to prepare, initiate or wage aggressive wars. He attended none of the important conferences when Hitler revealed piece by piece those plans for aggression, nor can knowledge be conclusively inferred from the positions he held." Finally, Your Honour, the third element: Necessary and reasonable measures. The time has come for the Defence to try once again to explain our many requests about the body of law which applies to those proceedings. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal and of the ICTR is very clear on that point: The command responsibility is responsibility for failure to carry out your duties, and I just refer Your Honour to paragraph 35 of the Bagilishema Appeals Chamber judgement which says this: "A military commander or a civilian superior may therefore be held responsible if he failed to discharge his duties as a superior either by deliberately failing to perform them or by culpably or willfully disregarding them." Our question was this from the beginning of this trial: Where was Mr. Halilovic to turn to determine its obligation according to the Prosecution? Which body of law was he to have failed to comply with? Based on what body of law is the Prosecution requesting that he had to request a status report, whatever that means? What body of law request suggests that he should have sent written instructions about the choice of troops? What body of law requires of Mr. Halilovic that he had to perform a security assessment in Grabovica? That question, Your Honour, was ours for the length of the proceedings, now it becomes yours. What body of law will the Trial Chamber turn to, to make that determination? What body of law makes Sefer Halilovic a murderer, according to the Prosecution? Common Article 3. The Prosecution yesterday appeared to suggest that the Defence was challenging the customary status of that. No, certainly not. It is part of customary international law. This is the basics. Yes, it's customary international law; yes, the ICJ has recognised it; this Tribunal has said so. It applies both in international and internal armed conflict. We don't question that fact. But Common Article 3 has nothing to do with the responsibility of Mr. Halilovic. It is a mini-Geneva Conventions which provide for the minimum guarantees of victims of war and it's been interpreted here as criminalising a number of conduct: Rape, murder, and a number of others. It has nothing to do with the responsibility of a commander. What about treaties then? Geneva Conventions? Nothing relating to the duties and responsibility of a commander. What about the additional protocol? Additional Protocol II, well there's nothing about commanders again. Additional Protocol I, however, contains such article, Article 87. I think I may leave on the side the issues of whether or not this protocol would be applicable concerning the nature of the armed conflict which the Prosecution seeks to apply. But it just says this, it's paragraph 3, that "The high contracting party will have to ensure that commanders should initiate such steps as unnecessary to prevent such violations of the conventions or this protocol, and where appropriate to initiate disciplinary or penal action against violators thereof." It's very clear, Your Honour, from the commentary of the ICRC that the way in which this should be organised was left to states and that several states during the negotiation made it clear they were not ready to bind themselves at the international level as to how this should happen. Furthermore, there is no sign in the Additional Protocol of any of the obligations and duties mentioned by the Prosecution. They are inventions. They do not exist in law. I'll just note in passing the attempt yesterday by the Prosecution to now suggest, as they have in their final brief, that the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols were binding on Bosnia at the relevant time. If that was true, this should have been done in evidence. This wasn't the case. What we're saying is if the Prosecution is serious about proving that matter, they missed the time. They have yesterday showed a letter, apparently the letter of ratification, from the Bosnian authorities. Well, it would appear from other cases that those letters did not necessarily reach the Swiss government until much later, much after it was sent. We are not in a position to ascertain when those letters were received by the Swiss government and whether the instruments were ratified at the relevant time, but this is not our obligation. This is the Prosecution's obligation. What about domestic practice, Your Honour? Is there anything relevant to the list of obligation put forward by the Prosecution? Nothing, nothing the Prosecution could point to and certainly nothing which was applicable to Mr. Halilovic. What about the custom, then? Not a shred of evidence either, more opinion juris. Precedent? Well, the Prosecution has conceded yesterday that there was no precedent which would support their case and we fully agree with that. However, there is a case which may be of great assistance to the Chamber, and that's the Toyoda case which is a case very similar to the present one and we invite the Chamber to look at this case. Well, in that case, where is the Trial Chamber to turn to in the absence of the law, as we see it? Well, the life of a soldier, and particularly the life of a soldier at war, is not a moral assignment. The rules must be clear, because if there is a breach he must be able to react and he must be able to react promptly and appropriately. A British court mentioned that "no sailor and no soldiers can carry with him a library of international law." That's the Peleus trial. That would be a heavy library indeed. What you're being asked to do by the Prosecution in this case is to invent new law, to enter new territories unchartered, and that's not the law. You're being asked to create law for Sefer Halilovic. We also draw the Trial Chamber to the issue of the principle of legality which is to be found in the Ojdanic interlocutory decision at paragraph 37. And I will jump forward to what would appear to be the last issue we will have the time to deal with. But command responsibility is responsibility for the failure of the commander, a personal dereliction which has been said to amount to "wanton immoral disregard of the actions of his subordinates." He is not to be held responsible for whatever failure may be attributed to his subordinates or to anyone else. Any other interpretation of the law, the high command court said, go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law. Therefore, once his obligation to act has been triggered, the commander has to act. But he doesn't have to take the steps himself. Article -- the ICRC commentary of Article 87 says this: "The commander has certain duties, but this does not mean that he must do everything himself and in fact a great deal of leeway has been left to his subordinates." And I refer to our quote in the brief in that regard. The Prosecution seems to say that the order of Mr. Halilovic to Namik Dzankovic to investigate was not enough. There was more to do. There was a status report to ask. The order should have been written. Well, we've pointed out that this is not the law. But furthermore, to repeat ourself, we direct Your Honour to a statement of legal advisor to the Office of the Prosecutor Mr. Bill Fenerick in an article which he contributed in the Otto Trifetterer ICC commentary, where he says this: "A commander is unlikely to have direct and complete control over a military or civil judicial system. Even the most high-ranking commander is unlikely to be able to do more than refer matters to authorities responsible for investigation and prosecution of offences." But that's not only the view of the otherwise excellent Mr. Fenrick, that's also the view of this Tribunal in Blaskic, Stakic, and Aleksovski. "The obligation to prevent or punish may under some circumstances be satisfied by reporting the matter to the competent authorities." Finally, in unexpected places, perhaps, the Supreme Court of Florida said this: "A commander may fulfil his duty to investigate and punish wrongdoers if he delegates this duty to a responsible subordinate. The commander has a right to assume that rights entrusted to a responsible subordinate will be properly executed." Finally, Your Honour, and very briefly: Even if an accused were to be found to have failed in his duty, that duty must be also blatant, as it has been named in the past. That is, one that is so clear and obvious that the accused must be aware of the criminal character and the grave criminal character of his offence. President Cassese at the time said that Article 7.3 was intended for what he called "system criminality, that is, the obnoxious involvement of policymakers in widespread and systematic disregard of human rights." That is the standard. The last requirement, and simply to direct Your Honour to the relevant pages. Yesterday the Prosecution suggested that the requirement of causality was based on no more than an article by Professor Trifetterer? And the writing of co-counsel for Sefer Halilovic. We invite you to look at paragraph 592 to 595 of the Defence final brief, where Your Honour will find plenty of authority for that submission. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess that's the end of the closing arguments on the part of the Defence. Could I ask you a question, Mr. Mettraux, since we still have a few minutes left. Is that your position in order to establish the mens rea of the commander's responsibility, the commander should share the intent of his subordinate who committed a particular crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have a different task or a different hat today than I have at other time. And my counsel here today obliges me today to answer that the law of this Tribunal is that the commander only needs to have known of the mens rea of his subordinates. The more academic hat that I sometimes wear tend to think that more has to be established. But the academic has been defeated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Another issue is that if it's the intention of the Defence to file the book of authorities, I believe that the same criteria is also applied to your side as well as to the Prosecution, that is: We only need the table of the contents rather than the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And also, the time period is the same, that is within one week's period. Yes, I believe that's all for this morning's sitting. And as I announced before, we'll resume at quarter past 3.00 this afternoon for any rebuttal arguments. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as stated in our Scheduling Order, that each party will have 30 minutes for rebuttal argument, and I have to stress that it is not an opportunity for the parties to reinforce their argument but just to rebut whatever they are not expected in the briefs but appeared in their closing argument. Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Re will go first, to cover four legal points and then I'll follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank. Mr. Re, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just going to address -- thank you, Your Honours -- several points raised in the address of my learned colleague Mr. Mettraux a bit earlier. The first point I wish to respond to, bearing of course Your Honour's direction not to raise fresh matters or to go over things from earlier, is my learned colleague referred at page 85 of the transcript to the Kvocka appeal, and which he said that he referred to Kvocka and said that he was also seen and heard giving orders to camp guards, and despite all of the above he was found not to be in effective control of the alleged perpetrator. The finding was upheld on appeal. Reluctantly, I have to say that that is not quite the position at all. Any reference to the appeal in this respect is completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours. There is no translation for Mr. Halilovic at this moment. I apologise to Mr. Re. It's just been brought to my attention that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Shall we try it again? Do you hear it? Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I direct -- or sorry, I refer the Trial Chamber to pages 47 to 52, paragraphs 136 onwards of the judgement. It was not an issue on appeal. It was not upheld on appeal because it was not a 7(3) case on appeal. On appeal it was only a 7 -- case under Article 7(1). That is my first point. The second one is the argument at page 87 of today's transcript, referring to orders issued by Mr. Halilovic after the crimes in Grabovica and the arguments that these are evidentiarily irrelevant. Those was the word used. The Prosecution completely refutes that. Any orders made by the accused within the time period, the temporal time period charged in the indictment are relevant circumstantially or directly to proving his effective control at the time. You could do it through looking at the combination of evidence of orders issued before and afterwards to prove that he had effective control at the time. And we certainly invite the Trial Chamber to do that. The third issue was that of -- raised again at page 88 within the Defence submissions of the role of the Chief of Staff. The high command case may well say the Chief of Staff had no command authority. It's not an issue in this case. A Chief of Staff has whatever authority a commander gives him or her at the time. The evidence is clear that Mr. Halilovic had certain command authorities in Operation Neretva and he exercised them. The high command case cannot be used for an authoritative position in relation to all cases involving a Chief of Staff. It must be decided on a case-by-case basis. The next point is at paragraph -- sorry, page 89 of today's transcript in which Mr. Mettraux referred to paragraph 41 of the Blaskic appeals judgement. I refer Your Honours to that very paragraph. The submission of the Defence was to tie it to Article 7(3). Blaskic Appeals Chamber is only referring to Article 7(1). I won't read it on to the record because of time, but I refer Your Honours to that paragraph and to bear in mind when you go to the transcript that paragraph 41 and Blaskic at that point is only 7(1) because he was not convicted in relation to 7(3) on appeal. The next point I take Your Honours to is at page 89 of the transcript where Mr. Mettraux referred again to the issue where he said that Mr. -- seemed to be confusing two issues; that is, the knowledge which a commander must have, and that of the intention of the perpetrators of the crime. And over the page the submission was: "The Prosecution will have to show that Mr. Halilovic knew at the relevant time of all of the elements of the definition of murder, including the specific state of mind required for that offence. They failed." That in our submission is an incorrect summation of the law. We said yesterday that murder does not require -- is not a specific intent crime. I refer Your Honours to the Krnojelac appeals judgments and specifically at paragraphs 187. There are only three specific intent crimes: Genocide, torture and persecution. The test in Krnojelac, it's four lines, is whether the person in charge, that's Krnojelac, "had sufficient information to alert him to the risk that inhumane acts and cruel treatment were being committed against the non-Serb detainees because of their political or religious affiliation. The Trial Chamber therefore committed an error of fact." The point in Krnojelac was that it was referring to a specific intent crime, namely torture, and the commander there needing to know of the specific intention of the perpetrators. It is not the case in a case of murder, which is simply not a specific intent crime. Murder, it is very clear, the case law of this Tribunal, is -- can be committed by indirect or direct intent. Also in addition, in relation to Krnojelac, the commander under 7(3) would not actually need to know that torture was actually happening, merely that the circumstances were sufficient to give the person notice, the necessary notice, to act. They do not need to know of the specific crime occurring at the time. The next point is in relation to the international -- sorry, the adoption of the -- the ratification -- this is at page 95, of the Geneva Conventions by the Bosnian government. Mr. Mettraux said: "We are not in a position to ascertain whether those letters were received by the Swiss government and whether the instruments were ratified at the relevant time. But this is not our obligation," and the time, he says, has passed for us to say so. With respect to our colleagues on the other side, that is just errant nonsense. The letter, the notification says, this is the Swiss government saying on the 31st of December, 1992, Bosnia deposited with the Swiss Federal Council the declaration of succession, and they made it in accordance with the -- and the Swiss government then notified the other parties. It hasn't been an issue throughout the trial, as far as we know, that Bosnia was not a party to the conventions, and it's something which you can take judicial notice, and I can certainly hand up the letter if the Trial Chamber wants it, and it's certainly available in the ICTY library. Very easy to find. Another legal error is at page 91 of the transcript where Mr. Mettraux said: "In addition to the knowledge already mentioned, the accused must be shown to have intended not to act as he was required to do, with or without that knowledge." In our submission, that is an inaccurate summation of the law. The -- and it brings it close to making it into a 7(1) intention or mens rea. The mens rea here is the notice, the knowledge; the intention is not required at that point. The trigger, that's the trigger, for the omission. They then go on to say: "We've pointed out the failure of the accused must be intentional in the sense of being both voluntary and deliberate." Again, in our submission, that is mischaracterisation of the law. It does not need to be deliberate in that sense, in the same sense it has to be for a 7(1) offence. It is the trigger -- it does not have to be deliberate. It has to be an omission. The omission does not have to be deliberate in the sense that it is something which you deliberately intend to omit. Knowing it and you omit to do so - it may sound like I'm splitting hairs here a little bit - but we say they are putting it too high in that sense by putting it in those way [sic]. The final point I make is page 97, my learned friend Mr. Mettraux in his final comment said: "Even if an accused were to be found to have failed in his duty, the duty must be blatant, one that is so clear and obvious that the accused must be aware of the criminal character and the grave criminal character of his offence." Again, our submission is the Defence is overstating it. There is absolutely no requirement under case law or customary law that the criminal offence must be grave in offence. That may well be a characterisation to invoke the jurisdiction of this Tribunal but -- serious violation of IHL had been committed but it forms no part of customary law. Those are my submissions on the legal points.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm going to address a number of points, as many as we can in the time remaining. The first one is the indication that footnote 549 was incorrect, that the -- it was a post facto offer of military police. We checked that and they are absolutely right. It is incorrect and we apologise for that. Next, counsel asked why Halilovic did not have anything to do with the 4th Corps. I will quote him. The -- on page 20, going into 21: "The operation was about Mostar. That's where the 4th Corps were. How can it be that Halilovic commanding those units did not have anything to do with the 4th Corps at that time? But the answer is resolved if Delalic retained command power for himself. In that way, coordination between the two parts of the operation is maintained." If, however, we go to Exhibit 289 at page 43, which is the book of Sevko Hodzic, that as you recall is the reporter that Sefer Halilovic brought along with him to record his glory. It says: Did Arif Pasalic set off today with the 4th Corps, I asked Sefer? No, he did not. He will receive an order on when he needs to move, Sefer replied." And then if you go down to the bottom of the page, the reporter says: "Of course I spoke to Pasalic on a number of occasions about Operation Neretva. I participated in the planning of this operation in Sarajevo, Pasalic said. Bilajac, Sefer and I, and partly Commander Delic who signed it. However Sefer was late to come out of Sarajevo." He participated in the planning of the operation with the accused. Allegations that the 4th Corps were not involved is in conflict with the statements of the commander of the 4th Corps, plus we also have two and possibly three letters from the commander of the 4th Corps sent to the forward command post, the IKM at Jablanica. Based on the book of Hodzic who records the statement of Pasalic. Pasalic was involved in operation Neretva. And he was involved because it concerned Mostar which was his area of responsibility. Now, counsel further states that it's unlikely that either President Izetbegovic or Commander Delic would appoint Halilovic to command authority. First of all, you have a transcript where Izetbegovic makes it clear that that's exactly what he didn't -- what he didn't -- going to do, or he wasn't planning to do. It's a mistake in the transcript. If we go to P281, which is the book of Sefer Halilovic, "Cunning Strategy," on page 4 of the exhibit, in the first paragraph: "At the meeting, Alispahic said the president has given you the green light for the operation in order to help Mostar. I am putting the 50 strong Lasta detachment at your disposal. Every one rejoiced and immediately started planning Lasta's participation." The president was aware of what was going on. Next, counsel refers to Ramiz Delalic, commonly known as Celo, as a criminal, a bad one, a manipulator and so on. This type of person -- this is the type of person, this criminal, bad one, manipulator, that the defendant brought to Herzegovina. If he was so worried about this criminal he wouldn't have brought him to Herzegovina unless he didn't care, and that's what we suggest, he just didn't care. He brought this criminal to Herzegovina. Now, should this Court believe anything that this criminal says? We have had criminals testify here before, in the Bosanski Samac case we had a criminal who had committed murder, who had committed rape, who had committed torture, who had beat 500 or more people, and that person testified, and how did the court look at that? The way they've looked at other murderers that have testified before this court, and this Chamber we suggest should do the same. You rely on those portions of testimony that are corroborated. When there is corroboration for that testimony, it should be viewed just like any other testimony. Just like the Court in the Bosanski Samac case, which is Prosecutor versus Simic, Tadic and Zaric relied on that particular person in that case. Counsel claims that no information was introduced as to the IKM and its powers but I would just invite counsel and I invite the Court really to look to the testimony of Selmo Cikotic on February 23, pages 42 to 48; Salko Gusic, February 2nd, 62 to 64; and Salko Gusic, February 8th at 99 to 100 in which they discussed the IKM. And I'll just -- the last sentence or the last two sentence of Salko Gusic says on February 8th: "So by definition, the forward command post is smaller than a command. It contains only as much personnel and equipment as is necessary to effect these functions of command and control." Sorry, control and command. Now, during their argument, counsel indicated there are certain -- that some of the necessary measures which Prosecution stated in its closing brief and also in its argument were somewhat, if you want to call it, invented by the Prosecution. But let's look and see what is in the transcript. The security assessment. Where does the thought of the security assessment come from? It comes right from the record. Jusuf Jasarevic, on March 1, 2005, he's the one who talks about the duty to perform a security assessment. And talks in 86, 87, the need for a security assessment and how that security assessment would have prevented the billeting of those soldiers with those local civilians. And then he finishes off as he continues to speak that if they had to have been billeted there, there was no option, then based on that security assessment, actions would have been taken to protect those civilians, either move them, separated them from the soldiers, or taken certain action which we know weren't taken. Counsel also addressed certain failures or said that they would address certain failures that we claimed occurred at Grabovica and that they would answer them. And they said that there really was a security assessment. Karic, speaking with the elderly villagers, according to them constitutes a security assessment. We suggest that that doesn't constitute a security assessment. Going house to house and seeing some of the elderly villagers asking them, Do you mind troops staying here? That isn't a security assessment. That doesn't talk about the potential danger, that doesn't discuss the danger to the troops, the danger to the civilians, what sort of security needs to be installed or placed there for the protection of all. That was not a security assessment. And in fact, Karic never indicates in his testimony that he performed any sort of security assessment. Counsel also says that there was some supervision and refers to Karic's visit. That was a one- to one-and-a-half hour visit. One- to one-and-a-half hours during a period of, let's say, 30-plus hours, that those troops were there and then the crimes occurred, or 30 hours in the period that they first got there to maybe the end of the crimes. Maybe it's even as much as 36. One- to one-and-a-half hours in a 36-hour period, that does not constitute supervision. They were there to greet the soldiers and to distribute food. And that's what Dzankovic tells. He's passing out pies; he's taking them out of the trucks and bringing plates or tins of pies to the soldiers. That's not an act of supervision. There was testimony that Halilovic discharged his duties or fulfilled his responsibilities by speaking with Dzankovic. What does Jasarevic say? At page 32, on 3 March 2005: "Mr. Dzankovic, as a member of the inspection team in this case, had no competence, no power, and no authority because after all, he had never received an order from the commander that he could then see through. It would have been very difficult for him to find himself in a situation like that. I did try to explain a while ago about these circumstances so I don't think I should waste any more time now." He didn't even want to respond further. Again, as to whether or not Halilovic discharged his duties by notifying Dzankovic, he says, on the 4th of March, at page 47: "Q. You said you see no realistic possibility for Dzankovic doing anything without clear orders from a position of authority. That was one. One of the utterances that you made. Do you remember? "Yes, I remember the context. In my view, from the aspect of my professional mandate, Dzankovic was not the person who could carry out such complex tasks -- I'm sorry, such complex tasks in such a situation without having the resources at his disposal. When I say resources, I mean officers of the military security such as were available to aid either a brigade or corps. Further on, he should have had police officers, strong forces that were necessary in order to carry out an investigation and collection of relevant information that would enable for the proceedings to go on. That's one element." I said testimony previously; I referred to my submission. Just looking quickly before I move on with regard to Mr. Dzankovic, Mr. Dzankovic never filed one report where he indicated he interviewed one victim, where he interviewed one witness, where he did some on-scene analysis. He never did anything. Any work that was done was performed by the local police. Now, there was an issue raised as to effective control, and basically it was you can't have effective control of uncontrollable troops. But what do we know from the facts? These troops followed combat orders. They were good fighters. They had a relationship with Halilovic. Or their commanders had a relationship had Halilovic. He could speak to them. They might have been unruly when dealing with civilians and citizens but they followed their combat orders. Now, Karavelic, pages 156, 157 on April 18 addresses that point. What was the relationship like -- or sorry: "What was the relationship between the 1st Corps command and the 9th Motorised Brigade in 1993, in terms of command and control, that is, the issuing of orders by the corps command and how they were responded to by the 9th Motorised Brigade?" And his answer: "All orders issued during 1993 to the 9th Motorised Brigade by the command of the 1st Corps were issued to the commander of that brigade. I can say that, all orders which refer and which referred to the execution of combat activities in terms of defending the defence lines in the zone of responsibility and/or the execution of all kinds of combat operations that were ordered were carried out for the most part by the 9th Motorised Brigade, so that there were no real serious problems in respect to the execution of the basic tasks, the basic missions of the brigade. There were no such problems." This goes back to the issue once again. The issue was not their fighting abilities. The issue was not their ability to wage combat. Their issue was the mistreatment of civilians, which leads to the last point. When counsel says that there was no basis for concluding that there was any danger. Where was the danger? How would Halilovic know of the danger? When you have troops that have consistently mistreated civilians and you're sending to the area, even if it isn't Grabovica, you send them to the Jablanica area where there are civilians, and there are civilians from the enemy side, civilians whose relatives and friends they will be fighting against, you don't need any expert to say that there is a danger of harm, a danger of mistreatment or a danger of murder. That's self-evident, Your Honour. If there are any other points you'd like us to address, we would address them now. If not -- one moment, please. Sorry, one just quick point on page 108 of the transcript, line 40 it says "there is testimony that." I meant to say a Defence counsel submitted or made a submission that. Thank you. If there are no questions, that completes our rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours. Could I just indicate I think from Your Honour's -- from what Your Honours said our rebuttal is limited to that which has just flowed now because we had notice of what they said in their opening previously, so we will be short. I will I deal with my learned friend's last submission about when notice has got to arise. We did not get a time at which notice arose. You don't have such a time. Going in reverse order now, my learned friend said that you could draw a conclusion that Ramiz Delalic was able to be effectively controlled because he obeyed combat orders. And there is no dispute that he obeyed combat orders. The real problem is that he didn't obey any others. And what is at issue here is a material ability to be able to punish. In other words, what Halilovic is charged with is failing to punish Ramiz Delalic, and the effective control that needs to be established in that regard is a material ability to punish him. Now, that doesn't depend on him obeying combat orders. It depends on him obeying the other kind of orders such as to go along with an investigation, or to do normal things, to remain in the line of command and control. Halilovic's ability or anyone else's ability to give him combat orders does not determine the question. In fact it's, strictly speaking, irrelevant to the question. The issue is, as we dealt with in our brief, would he obey any others? And when he is standing directly in the way of the investigation, as he did, we say that what the Prosecution's pointed out there is exactly the problem. He just wouldn't comply unless it was a combat order, and his ability or his willingness to comply with combat orders is not relevant to his being effectively controlled in respect to punishment of any particular crime. Now, my friend made the point concerning Mr. Dzankovic and the effectiveness of the order given by Halilovic to him, and it was said by the Prosecutor that relying on Jusuf Jasarevic that Halilovic's order was not enough and that more support was needed to be given to Dzankovic. But in Exhibit D215 which is Dzankovic's report, Dzankovic asks for support. He asks for a mixed commission to be given and so on. And you have that order. And the person he asked was Jusuf Jasarevic himself, not Halilovic. Dzankovic's position was quite different it to that of Jasarevic. He thought it was Jasarevic who should have helped him. Jasarevic didn't help, at least was unable to help him in respect of that order. Jasarevic, of course, said didn't get that letter until a week later and that could be true. So I don't wish to blame Jasarevic. But what I wish to point out is that it's not a valid objection by the Prosecutor because when you turn to what Dzankovic thought should happen he didn't turn to Halilovic and he didn't ask him for those things. Nor at the time did Jasarevic ask Halilovic to do those things when he finally got the report from Dzankovic. Dzankovic sends his report requesting things to Jusuf Jasarevic. Jasarevic did not then say to Halilovic, Could you please look after this because it's your job? Your Honours, my learned friend raised an issue concerning the measures the Prosecution have outlined, and they said that the duty to perform a security assessment was not invented by them but arises out of the evidence of Jasarevic. Well, that could be true, Your Honour, it could be that it arose out of Jasarevic's evidence and we don't quarrel with it. All we'll say in response to that is that Mr. Karic did make a visit. If the Prosecution don't think that's a good security assessment. That's getting a long way away from war crimes. That's splitting arguments at the time. Karic did at the time what he thought was appropriate. He's a combat officer, he was in the area, and Jasarevic wasn't. But in any event, we are still remote from Halilovic. Because no one suggests that Halilovic was consulted by Karic on the content of that visit and what should be done, and Halilovic, as we've said, was entitled to rely upon the good faith and good behaviour of an experienced and one would say upright officer. As to the IKM, my learned friend raised an issue and said that you could look to the evidence of Messrs. Cikotic and Gusic. And that's quite true, you can look to that evidence. We'd just say you could look to Cikotic with some measure of good faith. Gusic you know will put whatever cast on that evidence will most avoid him being liable, and therefore, you'd prefer Cikotic to Gusic. But of course you're entitled to look at all the evidence and see what value it gives, and our point is that the Prosecutors decided not to call any expert evidence on that. My learned friend -- my learned co-counsel reminds me that there has been discussion of an IKM and its possible operation in the Hadzihasanovic case. If that's reflected in decisions, Your Honours might be entitled to look at it, but we should -- you should proceed on the evidence that's in this case. It was put that Ramiz Delalic was a criminal and that the Defence have now fallen into a very cunning strategy by the Prosecutor because by calling Delalic they force us to attack him and then they say, Ah-hah, we've revealed now what an evil man Delalic is and that just shows that Halilovic shouldn't have used him. But there is an easy answer to that one. Halilovic didn't know as much as you do. At that time, Ramiz Delalic was only a young man and what he'd done is to defend Sarajevo, perhaps in a slightly unorthodox way and not being in the line of command and control. At that time he hadn't perjured himself in court or become a major underworld figure. At the time when Halilovic knew Ramiz Delalic, and at the time when Delalic gave to Herzegovina, Delalic hadn't yet covered up a major crime in Grabovica. Halilovic didn't have the knowledge that the Prosecutors had. It's the Prosecutors who should have been on inquiry notice not to use a dangerous person, not Halilovic. It's they who would knew very well what he is, and it's they it would have used him to the detriment of their case and this trial. It's put that in relation to Ramiz Delalic, you can believe him if he's corroborated. Well, we put to you that's not right. Sometimes that is right. Sometimes you can get a crazy person or a bad witness. They can be corroborated; you can believe them. But Delalic knows the case. He's prepared it, he was here with his admirable interrupting lawyer, Mr. Karkin. He knows the documents here. If he happens to say something that's consistent with other evidence, that doesn't mean he's corroborated. It just means he's smart. It just means he knows about it. You can't believe him if he's corroborated because the likelihood is that he's just adopted that evidence. When it comes to the second-last question, it was said that Mr. Izetbegovic knew of the operation and gave it the green light. Well, that's probably true but that begs the question: Was Halilovic the commander of it or not? See, of course we agree with that. It does raise another interesting issue, of course. Well, in any event, I've not to go outside the questions and I won't. And finally, the Prosecution raised a issue concerning Pasalic, a comment by Halilovic that Pasalic will receive an order. That's a quote from the journalist Sevko Hodzic. And he's a decent witness, a person who basically came here and told the truth, so you would be entitled to act on that. But it doesn't mean it's an order by Halilovic that Pasalic is going to receive. That's the magic bit that the Prosecution miss. Pasalic might receive an order. But in any event, we've got the evidence from Budakovic and Najetovic, the people who were there from the 4th Corps who said, Well, we knew nothing about Neretva 93. We knew nothing about it. And those are the responses to the factual submissions by Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any legal responses?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: None, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Well, I believe that's all for the rebuttal arguments, and at this stage, I have some decisions to render. The Trial Chamber is seized of the Defence motion for confidential order re Rule 92 bis statements filed confidentially on the 18th of August, 2005, in which the Defence requests two 92 bis witness statements to be kept confidential. The Defence in its motion submits that it has indicated earlier that it would have no objection to lift the confidentiality of the Defence 92 bis statements once they were admitted into evidence. In light of the present motion, the Trial Chamber understands the Defence to object only to lift the protective measures for the two witnesses mentioned in the motion. The Defence submits that the Prosecution has indicated that it does not object to the motion being granted. The Trial Chamber finds there are reasons for remaining protective measures for the statements of both witnesses mentioned in the motion, and therefore grants the motion. The Trial Chamber finds there are no reason to remain the confidential status of the other admitted Defence 92 bis witness statements, and therefore lifts their confidential status. The Trial Chamber requests the Registrar to amend the status of the witness statements in accordance with this decision. I believe the Prosecution also have something to say with the confidentiality of their 92 bis statements. Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection to lifting the confidentiality of the two 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the confidentiality of those two 92 bis statements are lifted. And the third issue is about the Defence document we mentioned yesterday and this morning. Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that the document has now been provided to court staff, and I formally seek to tender that document, being a letter from the head of Bosnian -- sorry, this is -- it's a confidential letter, I'm sorry. From the head of Bosnian secret services, concerning a particular code. I offer that document for tender. The relevance of it is limited to this, that it -- Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit D437 was a document indicating that Halilovic was placed under surveillance, and on some documentation there is a particular number on which the Defence relied during evidence to indicate what level of threat, if you like, Halilovic constituted to the state to justify such measures, and evidence about that was led from two witnesses, Mr. Okovic and Mr. Alispahic. This letter indicates what is the meaning of that particular code, so it assists you to understand what was the reach of the measures employed against Halilovic and what, if any, inferences you choose to draw about the likelihood that he would be given command. That's the relevance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection. There is really no reason to keep it confidential since it's a -- it's now 12 years, 12-plus years later, and it could just go in with the other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D499.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter, but would you just permit me to go and approach Mr. Weiner very briefly? I don't want the Court to leave. Could I just go across and speak to him very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one quick matter. Learned counsel just reminded me. As you notice, one of the members of our team is not here. About a week and a half ago, Manoj Sachdeva, the fourth member of our team, his father passed away, and he really wanted to be here and participate in the arguments and assist, and we are very sorry that he's not able to be here. We would just like to publicly offer sympathies to Attorney Sachdeva and his family. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are very sorry to hear that. I think in the proceedings there are a lot of unexpected things happened. This Bench would like to offer its sympathies to that brilliant attorney at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we just join in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the oral proceedings of this case have come to an end. And as a principle, I believe that this Bench would like to uphold the finality of the proceedings. That is, no new evidence or motions shall be accepted or entertained unless there are some very extraordinary circumstances or unless there is something left over from the proceedings. I believe that this Bench will withdraw to consider and elaborate on the evidence received, taking into consideration the statements made by the counsels yesterday and today. It's very difficult to predict the exact date the final judgement will be rendered at this stage; but, however, we could say probably at the second week of November. That is more or less between 7th of November to 16th of November. At this occasion, the Bench would like to take this opportunity to thank both parties for their efforts to present their case, to assist us to understand this case. Our thanks also goes to all the people working for this case, including interpreters, court deputies, court reporters, guards, technicians and other people working for this case. Without their efforts, we could not finish our case in six or seven months. I believe that's all for this proceedings. I wish everybody have a good time and the hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.05 p.m.
